# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1811
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Period covered:** 1840s–1860s

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Civil Marriages 1677–1950** (FamilySearch collection 1571957) — 312,045 records, indexed + images — the primary civil marriage source for this period
- **Compiled Marriages 1700–1900** (collection 1502909) — 198,765 records, name-indexed but **no images**; use as a finding aid pointing to original records
- **Births and deaths (1840s–1860s):** No birth or death record collections overlapping this period were found online. Pennsylvania statewide death certificates don't begin until 1906. Church records are the primary alternative.

### Church Records
- **Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill County, 1840–1875** (FamilySearch vol. 004288771) — 198 images, **0% name-indexed, browse-only, English and German** ⚠️ Requires ability to read 19th-century German script
- Contact other denominational archives (Reformed, Catholic, Methodist, etc.) for non-Lutheran congregations — no other church volumes were returned

### Census Records
- **U.S. Federal Census, 1850–1860, Schuylkill County** (vol. 007621224) — 412 images, **96% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — the most accessible digitized record set for this county in the target period; start here
- The 1840 federal census was not surfaced in digitized volumes
- **Ancestry.com** also holds the 1850 Schuylkill County census (subscription required)

### Probate & Court Records
- **Probate Records, Schuylkill County, 1845–1880** (vol. 004812990) — 286 images, only **4% name-indexed but full-text searchable** — use the full-text interface
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images statewide, **0 indexed records — browse-only only**
- Originals held at the Schuylkill County courthouse

### Land Records
- No land record collections for Schuylkill County in this period were found online
- **Deed books** are held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds some series
- Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** (not federal-land); consult the FamilySearch Wiki for guidance

### Military Records
- Relevant conflicts: **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** and **Civil War (1861–1865)**
- No online military collections for Schuylkill County were found
- Records held at **NARA** (Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.) and the Pennsylvania State Archives

### Tax Records
- No tax record collections for the 1840s–1860s were returned online
- One Ancestry collection covers only 1768–1801 (predates this period)
- Originals likely at county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives

### Naturalization Records
- No online naturalization volumes for Schuylkill County were found
- Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in **any court of record** — check the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas records at the county courthouse

### Cemetery & Newspaper Records
- No digitized cemetery or newspaper collections were returned
- Check **FindAGrave**, **BillionGraves**, and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) directly

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Federal census 1850–1860; civil marriages; probate records; Lutheran church records | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County | Subscription |
| **Schuylkill County Courthouse** | Deed books, probate files, court records, naturalizations, tax records | In-person / mail inquiry |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | State-level records; some county microfilm | In-person / online finding aids |
| **NARA (Philadelphia & Washington, D.C.)** | Civil War, Mexican-American War service and pension records | In-person / NARA online |

---

## Records NOT Online
- Births and deaths (1840s–1860s) — no collections found; use church records
- Tax records for this period
- Military records for Schuylkill County
- Land/deed records
- Naturalization records
- Newspapers
- Probate images largely browse-only (no name index); Lutheran records browse-only and in German

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses** (FamilySearch vol. 007621224 — 96% indexed, full-text searchable) to build household profiles before searching less-accessible record types.
2. **For births and deaths**, Lutheran church registers are the first alternative — but they are browse-only images in German. Contact other denominational archives for non-Lutheran families.
3. **Probate records (1845–1880)** are full-text searchable but only 4% name-indexed — use the full-text search interface, not the name index.
4. **Compiled Marriages (collection 1502909)** is name-indexed but has no images — treat each hit as a pointer to the original record.
5. **German-language records:** Lutheran registers through the mid-1800s were commonly kept in German. Engage a German-language genealogical paleographer for vol. 004288771.
6. **Known record losses:** No specific losses for Schuylkill County were found in tools. Contact the **Schuylkill County Genealogical Society** and the **Pennsylvania State Archives** to inquire before concluding a record doesn't exist.

---

## Useful FamilySearch Wiki Pages (visit directly)
- [Schuylkill County Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)
- [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- [Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records)
- [Pennsylvania Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property)
- [Pennsylvania Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Census)

---

**Bottom line:** The most accessible records for Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s are the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses (fully searchable on FamilySearch), a statewide civil marriages collection, and probate records from 1845 onward. The most significant gap is the absence of online birth and death records for this period — church registers are the workaround, but they are largely unindexed and in German. Begin with the census as your anchor record, then branch out into church, probate, and courthouse records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties (source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (admitted to the Union June 1, 1792, originally organized from Virginia; 120 counties total)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the population tool for this place and period. Consult published census summaries or the FamilySearch Wiki for estimates.
- **Economy:** South-central Kentucky; primarily agricultural through 1840-1880. The region lies in the Cumberland Plateau foothills, with subsistence farming and small-scale commerce as dominant occupations. The Civil War (1861-1865) disrupted the local economy.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly settlers of Scots-Irish and English descent who arrived via the Wilderness Road and Cumberland Gap from Virginia and North Carolina. Limited international immigration relative to northern states.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian were the largest denominations in Kentucky before 1900 (source: Kentucky Church Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records). Smaller Protestant bodies including Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) and Cumberland Presbyterian were also present in south-central Kentucky.
- **Key historical events:** Kentucky was a border state during the Civil War (1861-1865), with divided loyalties among its residents — both Union and Confederate soldiers were raised from the county. Record losses occurred in 1838 and again in 1871 due to courthouse disasters (Pulaski County Genealogy wiki).

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County was formed December 10, 1798 from Lincoln County and Green County. Records for events before 1799 in the area that became Pulaski County are held in **Lincoln County** and **Green County**.
- No boundary changes to Pulaski County during the 1840-1880 period are recorded in the tool results. Boundaries appear stable throughout the target window.

## Available record types

All records in Kentucky were kept at the county level unless otherwise stated. There were no state-level vital records during 1840-1880 and no Kentucky state census at any time.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date and level:** County-level birth and death registration began in practice in 1852-1853, under a law that assigned registration to county tax assessors. This system was **not continuous**: it applied only during 1853-1862 and again during 1874-1878 within the target period. It lapsed during the Civil War and was not revived consistently until 1892-1910. Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until 1911, with general compliance achieved by 1917. County-level marriage registration dates from county formation (1799) and was continuous. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records)
- **What exists within 1840-1880:**
  - Marriage bonds and licenses: 1799 onward, continuous at the county level
  - Birth records: county level 1853-1862 only (then 1874-1878), with minimal compliance — many events went unregistered
  - Death records: county level 1853-1862 only (then 1874-1878), with minimal compliance
- **Where held:** Pre-1911 county-level records at the Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort, and the Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street #208, Somerset, KY 42502). Marriage bonds and consent forms 1799-1871 are digitized on FamilySearch (per Pulaski County Genealogy wiki). Post-1871 marriage records remain physical at the courthouse.
- **Gaps:** 1840-1852 (no civil birth/death records); 1862-1874 (registration lapsed, Civil War); 1878-1880 (no active registration). Compliance throughout the registration windows was minimal.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials, marriages); family Bibles; cemetery records; newspaper marriage and death notices; mortality schedules attached to the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic (Pulaski County falls within the Catholic Diocese of Lexington area). Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) and Cumberland Presbyterian also present. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, funerals/burials, confirmations, membership lists, and church minutes.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch: "Kentucky Church Records, 1818-1995" (index and images, incomplete); "Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839-1960" (index only); "Kentucky Marriages, 1785-1979" (index only); "Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970" (index only). These are partial collections — coverage for any specific Pulaski County congregation is not guaranteed.
  - Pulaski County Historical Society (Somerset): holds the most comprehensive local collection of church records and newspaper obituaries.
  - FamilySearch Library: microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations.
  - Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort): manuscript church records.
  - Denominational archives: Southern Baptist Historical Library (Nashville); Methodist conference archives; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); Diocese of Lexington (Catholic).
  - Active local congregations may still hold their own pre-1880 records.
- **Language:** English
- **Access levels:** FamilySearch church collections are partially indexed + images ("Kentucky Church Records") or index-only (christenings, marriages, deaths). Records held only at local congregations or the Pulaski County Historical Society are physical only.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Pulaski County is enumerated from 1810 onward. Enumerations within the target period: 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880. Mortality schedules (deaths in the preceding year) accompany the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations.
- **State census:** Kentucky did not take a state census at any point. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy)
- **Other enumerations:** None identified in tool results.
- **Access:** The collections_search and volume_search tools returned 0 results in this session (service issue; see Coverage note in the Repository guide). The Ancestry external link confirms U.S. Federal Census records are available on Ancestry.com. FamilySearch holds indexed federal census records for Kentucky for all decades 1840-1880, but no specific collection IDs were returned by the tools in this session. Mortality schedules are on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

**Coverage note:** The collections_search, volume_search, and catalog_search tools all returned 0 results in this survey session for both Pulaski County and Kentucky — this appears to be a service-level place-resolution issue rather than a confirmed absence of digitized collections. The FamilySearch collections listed above are derived from the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched directly. The researcher should search FamilySearch directly for additional Kentucky and Pulaski County collections not captured in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799 | In-person or written request |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset | Church records, obituary clippings, surname vertical files, cemetery surveys | Contact for hours; in-person |
| Kentucky Dept. for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records, pre-1911 vital records | In-person; some records available by mail request |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, newspapers, genealogical collections, Civil War records | In-person |
| University of Kentucky Special Collections, Lexington | Local histories, manuscripts | In-person |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; many records digitized on FamilySearch |
| National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region | Federal census originals, military service/pension files, naturalization, passenger lists | In-person at regional facility; many records online |

## Records NOT online
- Deed books at Pulaski County Courthouse (person-to-person land transfers) — physical or KDLA microfilm only
- County court order books — physical at courthouse; check KDLA microfilm
- Birth and death civil records for all years outside the registration windows (the majority of 1840-1880)
- Post-1871 marriage records (courthouse physical; FamilySearch holds only through 1871)
- Records of most individual church congregations not covered by the partial FamilySearch collection
- Pulaski County Historical Society surname vertical files and newspaper obituary clippings — physical only, in Somerset
- School records — physical at local repositories

## Known record losses
- **1838:** A disaster at the Pulaski County Courthouse destroyed some records. The specific record types lost are not identified in the tool results. Early deed books, court order books, and any birth or death records from before 1838 may be affected.
- **1871:** A second courthouse disaster destroyed additional Pulaski County records. Marriage bonds and consent forms (FamilySearch holds 1799-1871 — those that survived to be microfilmed are online), along with probate files and court records from the 1799-1871 period, may have gaps.
- (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)

**Substitutes for lost records:** Ante-bellum tax lists (Ancestry); church records; newspaper legal notices; land deeds that reference family members; probate inventories that name heirs; and any records re-recorded after the fires.

## Research tips
- **Marriage bonds are the most reliable vital record type for 1840-1880.** County-level marriage registration was continuous from county formation (1799); the early series (1799-1871) is on FamilySearch. This is the primary civil record for a marriage during this period. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Birth and death records are fragmentary.** Civil registration applied only during 1853-1862 and 1874-1878, with minimal compliance. For births and deaths outside those windows — the majority of the target period — church records, cemetery inscriptions, and mortality schedules are the primary sources. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records)
- **Use tax lists as census substitutes.** Annual county tax lists (Ancestry, Pulaski County) place individuals in the county year by year. They are especially critical for 1840-1852 and 1862-1874 when neither civil registration nor a new census exists. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Account for record losses in 1838 and 1871.** Do not assume that a missing courthouse record means the event did not occur. Use church records, tax lists, deeds, and newspapers to reconstruct facts that may have been destroyed. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Kentucky is a state-land state.** The metes-and-bounds land system and grants from both Virginia (before 1792) and Kentucky (after 1792) are key. Search FamilySearch for Kentucky Land Office records (1700-1955) before assuming no land patent exists. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property)
- **Civil War research requires checking both sides.** Union service and pension records are at NARA (Record Group 94); Confederate records are also at NARA (Record Group 109). Kentucky Confederate pension applications are at KDLA. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy)
- **No Kentucky state census exists.** The researcher must rely on federal decennial enumerations (1840-1880) plus annual tax lists for intercensal years. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy)
- **Pre-1799 records:** Events in the area before Pulaski County's formation in 1798 will be found in Lincoln County and Green County records. (Source: place_search_all tool result)
- **Check the Pulaski County Historical Society first for local resources.** The surname vertical files and newspaper obituary collection are not online and are a unique local resource.
- **Neighboring counties:** The neighboring counties table was not returned by the wiki_place_page home section (which returned only generic content). Families near Pulaski County's borders may have generated records in adjoining counties. Consult the Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy) for the neighboring counties list and search those courthouses as well.

Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

The Alabama region around 1800 was **not yet Alabama** — it was the **Mississippi Territory** (organized 1798), and the Mobile district remained under **Spanish colonial rule until 1813**. Alabama statehood was still nearly two decades away. Key facts for this period:

- **No civil vital records** (no civil birth, marriage, or death registration)
- The only formal county in the area was **Washington County** (formed 1800); most Anglo-American settlement surged after the Creek War of 1813–1814

## Record Types & Repositories

| Record Type | Where Held |
|---|---|
| **Territorial court & land files** (Mississippi Territory) | FamilySearch — 3 browse-only digitized volumes (not name-indexed) |
| **Early county deeds & probate** (from 1803) | County courthouses; Alabama Department of Archives & History |
| **Territorial land grants** | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808** (substitute for federal census) | Alabama Department of Archives & History, Montgomery |
| **Baptist & Methodist church registers** | Individual churches; historical societies |
| **Mobile colonial Catholic registers** (French/Spanish era) | Archives in France & Spain; copies at Library of Congress |

## Critical Search Tip

Search under **Mississippi Territory** records, *not* Alabama — searching for Alabama-labeled records for 1800 will miss nearly everything, because the political jurisdiction was entirely different.

## Recommended Next Steps

1. Identify which specific county or pre-county district your ancestor was in — this determines which territorial or early county records apply.
2. Run a research plan targeting the most likely record types (land grants and territorial court files are usually the richest sources for this era).

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, c. 1790–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Alabama region was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 until 1817, when the Alabama Territory was organized. Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** Mississippi Territory capital was Washington (near Natchez); Alabama Territory capital was St. Stephens.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, emerging cotton cultivation (especially after 1813), and commerce through the Mobile port. The Mobile River system was the main trade artery.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (large interior portions); Anglo-American settlers arriving from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee after 1798; French Creole community in the Mobile area; African American enslaved population; Spanish and other European settlers in Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area, established under French and Spanish rule); Baptist and Methodist circuit-riding churches among Anglo-American settlers; some Presbyterian congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory organized 1798; Spanish cession of Mobile 1813; Creek War 1813–1814 (opened central Alabama to American settlement); Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood 1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1798:** The Mobile area was French (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780), then Spanish (1780–1813). The interior was nominally under Georgia and U.S. territorial claims.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized; initially a narrow strip along the 31st and 32nd parallels.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to include more of present-day Alabama.
- **1812:** Further expansion added the remainder of present-day Alabama to the Mississippi Territory.
- **1813:** The United States seized Mobile from Spain, bringing the Mobile District under American authority.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama statehood.
- Records created around 1800 fall under the Mississippi Territory (and under Spanish jurisdiction for the Mobile area until 1813). Before 1804, only the southernmost strip of present-day Alabama was formally within the Mississippi Territory.

## Available record types

Note: Around 1800 the Alabama region had very limited civil infrastructure. Most record types described below did not begin until after the territory was more fully organized (post-1804) or after specific counties were formed.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey — all four wiki_place_page sections resolved to a generic fallback page rather than an Alabama-specific article. The earliest civil marriage records available on FamilySearch begin in 1809 (county level).
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registration for this period. County marriages begin in 1809 at the county level: Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (FamilySearch collection 1598408, 612,345 records, 306,172 images).
- **Where held:** County courthouses once formed; territorial records at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No civil registration for any vital events around 1800. Pre-1809 vital events are not captured in civil records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (Baptist, Methodist, Catholic) are the only contemporaneous source for vital events around 1800.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, dating to French and Spanish colonial era); Baptist and Methodist (among Anglo-American settlers after 1798); some Presbyterian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396, 156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images). Catholic records for the Mobile area dating to the colonial era are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives. French colonial records (including Catholic registers) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records for the Mobile District are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French and Spanish colonial periods are in French and Spanish respectively.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census is the first to include organized Alabama counties (then part of the Mississippi Territory). The 1800 census covered the Mississippi Territory but the Alabama portion was only partially organized and may not be fully enumerated.
- **Territorial censuses:** The FamilySearch wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records states that Mississippi Territory censuses were taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at ADAH in Montgomery.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District (pre-1813).
- **Access:** FamilySearch has the Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, index only — no images). FamilySearch also has Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (collection 1927171, 198,340 records, index only) covering the territorial period. The pre-1810 territorial censuses at ADAH are physical records not in any online indexed database.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** Washington County (formed 1800) is the earliest. FamilySearch volume_search returned a browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 004512890, 96 images) covering Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820 — browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. FamilySearch also has Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764, 438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images) beginning in 1809.
- **Territorial court records:** Volume_search returned a browse-only Alabama territorial court and land records volume (imageGroupNumber 004512889, 214 images, 1808–1819) and a Mississippi Territory land and court records volume (imageGroupNumber 004498712, 143 images, 1799–1817). Both are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** ADAH holds originals of territorial and early county records. County courthouses hold records from their date of formation.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal-land state — the rectangular (township-and-range) system, with grants through the federal General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal (General Land Office) for post-1804 grants. Pre-American land grants in the Mobile area were issued under French, British, and Spanish authority.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area), territorial land entries, county deeds, tax lists.
- **Date range:** First federal land sales in present-day Alabama began after 1804. Colonial grants predate 1798.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (collection 1919694, 312,450 indexed records, 156,225 images), covering the territorial period. Federal patents are at the BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). Colonial grants are in European archives (see Church records and Colonial records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812 (Gulf Coast theater); territorial militia against various threats 1798–1817.
- **Record types:** Militia rolls, federal service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service records and pension files. ADAH holds Alabama militia records. Fold3.com has military records available online.

### Cemetery records

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

The Alabama region around 1800 was not yet Alabama at all — it was the Mississippi Territory (organized in 1798), and the Mobile area remained under Spanish colonial rule until 1813. Because Alabama statehood was still nearly two decades away, there are no civil birth, marriage, or death records from this period; the government was barely organized, Washington County was the only formal county in the area (formed 1800), and most settlers arrived after the Creek War of 1813-1814. The records that do exist are territorial court and land files (three browse-only digitized volumes on FamilySearch, none of them name-indexed), early county deed and probate records beginning 1803, territorial land grants tracked through the BLM General Land Office website, church registers from Baptist and Methodist congregations among Anglo-American settlers, and — for anyone tied to Mobile — French and Spanish colonial Catholic registers held in archives in France and Spain with copies at the Library of Congress. The most important physical repository for this era is the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, which holds the Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) that substitute for the federal census in years when present-day Alabama was largely unenumerated. The main pitfall is searching Alabama-labeled records for 1800 when the correct search target is Mississippi Territory records.

The natural next step would be to identify which specific county (or pre-county district) your ancestor was in, since that determines which set of territorial or early county records applies — and to run a research plan targeting the record types most likely to name them.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, c. 1790–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Alabama region was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 until 1817, when the Alabama Territory was organized. Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** Mississippi Territory capital was Washington (near Natchez); Alabama Territory capital was St. Stephens.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, emerging cotton cultivation (especially after 1813), and commerce through the Mobile port. The Mobile River system was the main trade artery.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (large interior portions); Anglo-American settlers arriving from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee after 1798; French Creole community in the Mobile area; African American enslaved population; Spanish and other European settlers in Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area, established under French and Spanish rule); Baptist and Methodist circuit-riding churches among Anglo-American settlers; some Presbyterian congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory organized 1798; Spanish cession of Mobile 1813; Creek War 1813–1814 (opened central Alabama to American settlement); Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood 1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1798:** The Mobile area was French (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780), then Spanish (1780–1813). The interior was nominally under Georgia and U.S. territorial claims.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized; initially a narrow strip along the 31st and 32nd parallels.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to include more of present-day Alabama.
- **1812:** Further expansion added the remainder of present-day Alabama to the Mississippi Territory.
- **1813:** The United States seized Mobile from Spain, bringing the Mobile District under American authority.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama statehood.
- Records created around 1800 fall under the Mississippi Territory (and under Spanish jurisdiction for the Mobile area until 1813). Before 1804, only the southernmost strip of present-day Alabama was formally within the Mississippi Territory.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey — all four wiki_place_page sections resolved to a generic fallback page rather than an Alabama-specific article. The earliest civil marriage records available on FamilySearch begin in 1809 (county level).
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registration for this period. County marriages begin in 1809 at the county level: Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (FamilySearch collection 1598408, 612,345 records, 306,172 images).
- **Where held:** County courthouses once formed; territorial records at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No civil registration for any vital events around 1800. Pre-1809 vital events are not captured in civil records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (Baptist, Methodist, Catholic) are the only contemporaneous source for vital events around 1800.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, dating to French and Spanish colonial era); Baptist and Methodist (among Anglo-American settlers after 1798); some Presbyterian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396, 156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images). Locality guide written to the project (as **loc_001**). Here is the full report:

---

Before the United States existed, the land that is now Arkansas was controlled first by France (from 1686) and then by Spain (1763 to 1800), with virtually all European settlement concentrated at a single outpost called **Arkansas Post** on the lower Arkansas River. Because there was no civil government in any American sense, no birth certificates, marriage licenses, or death records were ever issued — the only records of baptisms, marriages, and burials were kept by the **Catholic Church at that post**. Spanish administrators also conducted periodic household census counts (called *padrones*), issued land grants, and kept military records, but these are all in French or Spanish, and most of the surviving originals are held in one of three places:

1. **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) — the primary state repository for colonial-era documents.
2. **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives** — holds surviving sacramental registers.
3. **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) — the mother archive for all Spanish colonial records; freely searchable through the PARES portal at [pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es).

### FamilySearch holdings
FamilySearch has digitized **one volume** from this period: approximately 64 pages of Spanish sacramental registers from Arkansas Post covering **1763–1800** (image group **008814402**). This volume is *not* name-indexed and must be browsed page by page, and the text is in Spanish.

### Suggested next steps
- **Browse the FamilySearch volume** (image group 008814402) page by page using the search-images agent.
- **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** for *padrones* (census lists), land grant records, and colonial correspondence.
- **Search the "Papeles de Cuba" series** via PARES (pares.mcu.es) — this is the primary Spanish administrative archive for the Gulf Coast and lower Mississippi Valley colonies and is likely to contain military lists, censuses, and land petitions naming Arkansas Post residents.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Before 1800 — French and Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by France; Spain took control under the Treaty of Paris in 1763
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas / Puesto del Arkansas), on the lower Arkansas River — the only significant European settlement in the region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (French: La Louisiane; Spanish: Luisiana), administered from New Orleans
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place-population tool for this period. The European-descended population was very small and almost entirely confined to Arkansas Post — primarily soldiers, traders, and their families, with surrounding Quapaw, Osage, and other Native nations.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, military garrison, limited subsistence agriculture
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and administrators, enslaved Africans, and Native American nations (Quapaw were the dominant neighboring nation)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — under both French and Spanish rule, Catholicism was the only officially permitted religion
- **Key historical events:** France founded Arkansas Post (1686); Seven Years' War / French and Indian War ended with the Treaty of Paris (1763), transferring Louisiana to Spain; Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post; Spain participated in the American Revolutionary War (1779); Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800) secretly returned Louisiana to France; Louisiana Purchase (1803) brought the region under US control

## Boundary changes
- The region that is now Arkansas had no fixed internal boundaries during this period. It was administered as part of the vast Province of Louisiana, governed from New Orleans.
- **French period (1686–1763):** All authority ran through the French colonial government in New Orleans. Records were created at Arkansas Post and in New Orleans.
- **Spanish period (1763–1800):** Spain reorganized Louisiana into an intendancy still centered on New Orleans. Arkansas Post functioned as a Comandancia (military command post) under the Spanish Governor-General of Louisiana.
- **After 1800:** Louisiana briefly returned to France, then was sold to the US in 1803. The Arkansas region moved through the Territory of Orleans (1804), the Missouri Territory (1812), and finally Arkansas Territory (1819) before becoming a state in 1836. Records created before 1800 were not re-filed under any of these later jurisdictions — they remained with their colonial custodians.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas did not return Arkansas-specific content on vital registration dates for this survey. All vital events were recorded by the Catholic Church.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the pre-1800 period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers at Arkansas Post are the only source for vital events in this period (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively, from the French founding period through the end of Spanish rule.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (and potentially confirmations). Registers record European settlers and Native Americans.
- **French period (pre-1763):** French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s, recording baptisms, marriages, and burials. Surviving registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission** ([Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)).
- **Spanish period (1763–1800):** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Spanish colonial sacramental registers for Arkansas Post (imageGroupNumber 008814402). It contains 64 images, covers 1763–1800, is in **Spanish**, has a record-searchable percentage of 0%, and is NOT full-text searchable. **It must be browsed image by image with no name index.** This is the only digitized record volume that FamilySearch's volume index returned for the pre-1800 Arkansas period.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763) and Spanish (1763–1800). Researchers must read these languages or use translation assistance.
- **Where held (physical):** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No federal census covers the pre-1800 period; the US census began in 1790 but Arkansas was not yet US territory.
- **Spanish colonial censuses (padrones):** Spain periodically enumerated the population of Arkansas Post. Padrones are household census lists recording the names of heads of household and family members. Surviving padrones are held at the **Arkansas History Commission** and at the **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** in Seville, Spain, with microfilm copies at the **Library of Congress** ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Access:** Physical repositories only. No FamilySearch indexed collection covers this material. The FamilySearch Arkansas Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index (collection 2085124) begins in 1819 and does not cover the pre-1800 period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish notarial practice required significant transactions (sales, contracts, wills) to be recorded by a notary. Civil and judicial records from the Arkansas Post Comandancia may include property disputes and estate matters.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Coverage:** Extremely sparse. The population was tiny and records are fragmentary. A person who died intestate at Arkansas Post likely left no probate record.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Under French and Spanish rule, land was granted by concession from the Crown or its colonial governor — not by a rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land concessions were issued by the Spanish colonial governor in New Orleans and recorded at Arkansas Post ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (land grants). Many were subsequently confirmed by the US government after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Where held (pre-1800 originals):** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **US confirmations (post-1803):** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records (glorecords.blm.gov). These US confirmation documents often name the original Spanish grantee, providing genealogically useful evidence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish garrison records at Arkansas Post; Spanish participation in the American Revolutionary War (1779–1783).
- **Record types:** Military muster rolls, soldier lists, officer reports, garrison correspondence.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville — particularly the 'Papeles de Cuba' series, which covers Spanish Louisiana military records. Microfilm at Library of Congress.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** No formal cemetery database covers this period. Catholic burials at Arkansas Post were recorded in the sacramental register.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries may appear in the FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402). No online cemetery index (FindAGrave, BillionGraves) covers pre-1800 Arkansas.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. The nearest newspapers were in New Orleans.
- **Value:** Not applicable for the pre-1800 Arkansas region.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** In the colonial period, movement to and from Arkansas Post was governed by French or Spanish administrative control, not modern immigration statutes.
- **Record types:** Travel permissions, passports (licencias de viaje) issued by Spanish colonial governors; administrative correspondence naming new arrivals.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for vessels arriving in New Orleans (the port serving the region) may name persons bound for Arkansas Post. These pre-1800 New Orleans arrival records are part of the broader French and Spanish Louisiana archive.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Taxation records may survive within Spanish administrative correspondence.
- **Where held:** AGI, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** The padrones (census lists) serve a comparable purpose for identifying the resident population.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Surviving notarial acts from Arkansas Post are at the Arkansas History Commission and the AGI.
- **Administrative correspondence:** Spanish colonial governors generated extensive correspondence that may name settlers at Arkansas Post by name. These are at AGI, Seville.
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories and articles in the *Arkansas Historical Quarterly* have transcribed and published portions of colonial-period records. Check WorldCat for published transcriptions before incurring travel costs.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only digitized volume: imageGroupNumber 008814402 (Spanish colonial sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800; 64 images; Spanish; 0% indexed; not full-text searchable) | Free |
| Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) | Digitized portions of the Archivo General de Indias, including 'Papeles de Cuba' (Spanish Louisiana records) | Free: http://pares.mcu.es |
| BLM General Land Office Records | US confirmations of Spanish land grants (post-1803, but names original Spanish grantees) | Free: https://glorecords.blm.gov |

No FamilySearch name-indexed collection covers the pre-1800 Arkansas period. The 3 collections returned by FamilySearch's Arkansas index (county marriages 1837–1957; Freedmen's Bureau 1865–1872; census substitutes index 1819–1870) all begin in 1819 or later. The 6 external links returned by FamilySearch's curated links tool are generic national resources and do not provide place-specific pre-1800 Arkansas coverage.

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume was returned by volume_search for Arkansas before 1800. That is the complete returned set (1 total result, no further pages).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, administrative records), French/Catholic sacramental register transcriptions | In-person or written inquiry: https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish-period Catholic sacramental registers | Contact Diocese archives for access |
| Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, Spain | Comprehensive Spanish colonial administrative, military, land, and notarial records for Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas Post | In-person (Seville) or PARES digital portal: http://pares.mcu.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of AGI records relating to Spanish Louisiana | In-person; identify specific microfilm rolls before visiting |
| Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Archives | Records of the broader Province of Louisiana, which administered Arkansas Post | In-person or online finding aids |
| Bureau of Land Management GLO | US confirmation records for Spanish land grants (post-1803) | Online: https://glorecords.blm.gov |

## Records NOT online

The following records exist but are not available in any searchable online database:

- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for Arkansas Post
- French-period Catholic sacramental registers (those not in the FamilySearch browse volume)
- Spanish land concession records (original grants at AGI and Arkansas History Commission)
- Spanish military muster rolls and garrison records
- Notarial records from Arkansas Post
- Administrative correspondence naming residents of Arkansas Post

The one digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) exists online but must be browsed image by image in Spanish with no name index.

## Known record losses

- Record survival from pre-1800 Arkansas is sparse. The population at Arkansas Post was very small, and not all records survived the transfers of sovereignty from France to Spain (1763), back to France (1800), and then to the United States (1803).
- Records that remained at Arkansas Post at the time of the Louisiana Purchase may have been dispersed or lost during the administrative transition.
- The primary surviving collections are those sent to Spain during colonial administration (now at AGI, Seville) and those retained in the Louisiana administrative chain (some of which eventually reached the Arkansas History Commission).
- There are no known substitute sources that fully compensate for the fragmentary nature of pre-1800 Arkansas records.

## Research tips

- **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) is your only online starting point.** It covers Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800, in Spanish, browse-only (64 images). Access it through the FamilySearch image viewer using that image group number. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Spanish (and French for pre-1763 records) is required.** All colonial-period records at Arkansas Post from 1763–1800 are in Spanish; earlier records are in French. Plan for translation assistance if needed.
- **The Archivo General de Indias (AGI) 'Papeles de Cuba' series is the primary source for Spanish Louisiana civil and military records**, including those from Arkansas Post. The PARES digital portal (http://pares.mcu.es) has digitized portions and is freely searchable. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Contact the Arkansas History Commission before planning a research trip.** They hold transcriptions and some originals and can advise on what has been indexed or published. https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission
- **Check published transcriptions first.** Arkansas colonial records have been partially transcribed in the *Arkansas Historical Quarterly* and in published volumes. Search WorldCat for these before incurring travel costs to Spain or Washington, DC.
- **Search adjoining Louisiana repositories.** The broader administrative jurisdiction for Arkansas Post was New Orleans. If your ancestor passed through or lived in Louisiana before or after residing in Arkansas, records may be found at the Historic New Orleans Collection, the Louisiana State Archives, and the New Orleans Notarial Archives. The neighboring jurisdictions to the south and east (the Red River districts and Natchitoches) also generated records for French and Spanish Louisiana that may name Arkansas settlers.
- **Spanish land grants may have been confirmed by the US after 1803.** Search the BLM GLO records (glorecords.blm.gov) for the US confirmation patent, which may describe the original Spanish grant and name the grantee. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Arkansas Post is now a National Memorial.** The Arkansas Post National Memorial (National Park Service) has interpretive materials and may point researchers to scholarly resources and bibliographies on the colonial period.
- **DNA evidence.** Given the very sparse documentary record, Y-DNA or autosomal DNA tested against French Creole and Spanish colonial Louisiana surname databases may help bridge gaps when documents cannot.

- **French period (1686–1763):** All authority ran through the French colonial government in New Orleans. Records were created at Arkansas Post and in New Orleans.
- **Spanish period (1763–1800):** Spain reorganized Louisiana into an intendancy still centered on New Orleans. Arkansas Post functioned as a Comandancia (military command post) under the Spanish Governor-General of Louisiana.
- **After 1800:** Louisiana briefly returned to France, then was sold to the US in 1803. The Arkansas region moved through the Territory of Orleans (1804), the Missouri Territory (1812), and finally Arkansas Territory (1819) before becoming a state in 1836. Records created before 1800 were not re-filed under any of these later jurisdictions — they remained with their colonial custodians.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas did not return Arkansas-specific content on vital registration dates for this survey. All vital events were recorded by the Catholic Church.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the pre-1800 period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers at Arkansas Post are the only source for vital events in this period (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively, from the French founding period through the end of Spanish rule.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (and potentially confirmations). Registers record European settlers and Native Americans.
- **French period (pre-1763):** French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s, recording baptisms, marriages, and burials. Surviving registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission** ([Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)).
- **Spanish period (1763–1800):** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Spanish colonial sacramental registers for Arkansas Post (imageGroupNumber 008814402). It contains 64 images, covers 1763–1800, is in **Spanish**, has a record-searchable percentage of 0%, and is NOT full-text searchable. **It must be browsed image by image with no name index.** This is the only digitized record volume that FamilySearch's volume index returned for the pre-1800 Arkansas period.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763) and Spanish (1763–1800). Researchers must read these languages or use translation assistance.
- **Where held (physical):** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No federal census covers the pre-1800 period; the US census began in 1790 but Arkansas was not yet US territory.
- **Spanish colonial censuses (padrones):** Spain periodically enumerated the population of Arkansas Post. Padrones are household census lists recording the names of heads of household and family members. Surviving padrones are held at the **Arkansas History Commission** and at the **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** in Seville, Spain, with microfilm copies at the **Library of Congress** ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Access:** Physical repositories only. No FamilySearch indexed collection covers this material. The FamilySearch Arkansas Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index (collection 2085124) begins in 1819 and does not cover the pre-1800 period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish notarial practice required significant transactions (sales, contracts, wills) to be recorded by a notary. Civil and judicial records from the Arkansas Post Comandancia may include property disputes and estate matters.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Coverage:** Extremely sparse. The population was tiny and records are fragmentary. A person who died intestate at Arkansas Post likely left no probate record.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Under French and Spanish rule, land was granted by concession from the Crown or its colonial governor — not by a rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land concessions were issued by the Spanish colonial governor in New Orleans and recorded at Arkansas Post ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (land grants). Many were subsequently confirmed by the US government after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Where held (pre-1800 originals):** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **US confirmations (post-1803):** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records (glorecords.blm.gov). These US confirmation documents often name the original Spanish grantee, providing genealogically useful evidence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish garrison records at Arkansas Post; Spanish participation in the American Revolutionary War (1779–1783).
- **Record types:** Military muster rolls, soldier lists, officer reports, garrison correspondence.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville — particularly the 'Papeles de Cuba' series, which covers Spanish Louisiana military records. Microfilm at Library of Congress.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** No formal cemetery database covers this period. Catholic burials at Arkansas Post were recorded in the sacramental register.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries may appear in the FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402). No online cemetery index (FindAGrave, BillionGraves) covers pre-1800 Arkansas.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. The nearest newspapers were in New Orleans.
- **Value:** Not applicable for the pre-1800 Arkansas region.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** In the colonial period, movement to and from Arkansas Post was governed by French or Spanish administrative control, not modern immigration statutes.
- **Record types:** Travel permissions, passports (licencias de viaje) issued by Spanish colonial governors; administrative correspondence naming new arrivals.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for vessels arriving in New Orleans (the port serving the region) may name persons bound for Arkansas Post. These pre-1800 New Orleans arrival records are part of the broader French and Spanish Louisiana archive.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Taxation records may survive within Spanish administrative correspondence.
- **Where held:** AGI, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** The padrones (census lists) serve a comparable purpose for identifying the resident population.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Surviving notarial acts from Arkansas Post are at the Arkansas History Commission and the AGI.
- **Administrative correspondence:** Spanish colonial governors generated extensive correspondence that may name settlers at Arkansas Post by name. These are at AGI, Seville.
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories and articles in the *Arkansas Historical Quarterly* have transcribed and published portions of colonial-period records. Check WorldCat for published transcriptions before incurring travel costs.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 browse-only digitized volume: imageGroupNumber 008814402 (Spanish colonial sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800; 64 images; Spanish; 0% indexed; not full-text searchable) | Free |
| Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) | Digitized portions of the Archivo General de Indias, including 'Papeles de Cuba' (Spanish Louisiana records) | Free: http://pares.mcu.es |
| BLM General Land Office Records | US confirmations of Spanish land grants (post-1803, but names original Spanish grantees) | Free: https://glorecords.blm.gov |

No FamilySearch name-indexed collection covers the pre-1800 Arkansas period. The 3 collections returned by FamilySearch's Arkansas index (county marriages 1837–1957; Freedmen's Bureau 1865–1872; census substitutes index 1819–1870) all begin in 1819 or later. The 6 external links returned by FamilySearch's curated links tool are generic national resources and do not provide place-specific pre-1800 Arkansas coverage.

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume was returned by volume_search for Arkansas before 1800. That is the complete returned set (1 total result, no further pages).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, administrative records), French/Catholic sacramental register transcriptions | In-person or written inquiry: https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish-period Catholic sacramental registers | Contact Diocese archives for access |
| Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, Spain | Comprehensive Spanish colonial administrative, military, land, and notarial records for Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas Post | In-person (Seville) or PARES digital portal: http://pares.mcu.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of AGI records relating to Spanish Louisiana | In-person; identify specific microfilm rolls before visiting |
| Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Archives | Records of the broader Province of Louisiana, which administered Arkansas Post | In-person or online finding aids |
| Bureau of Land Management GLO | US confirmation records for Spanish land grants (post-1803) | Online: https://glorecords.blm.gov |

## Records NOT online

The following records exist but are not available in any searchable online database:

- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for Arkansas Post
- French-period Catholic sacramental registers (those not in the FamilySearch browse volume)
- Spanish land concession records (original grants at AGI and Arkansas History Commission)
- Spanish military muster rolls and garrison records
- Notarial records from Arkansas Post
- Administrative correspondence naming residents of Arkansas Post

The one digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) exists online but must be browsed image by image in Spanish with no name index.

## Known record losses

- Record survival from pre-1800 Arkansas is sparse. The population at Arkansas Post was very small, and not all records survived the transfers of sovereignty from France to Spain (1763), back to France (1800), and then to the United States (1803).
- Records that remained at Arkansas Post at the time of the Louisiana Purchase may have been dispersed or lost during the administrative transition.
- The primary surviving collections are those sent to Spain during colonial administration (now at AGI, Seville) and those retained in the Louisiana administrative chain (some of which eventually reached the Arkansas History Commission).
- There are no known substitute sources that fully compensate for the fragmentary nature of pre-1800 Arkansas records.

## Research tips

- **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) is your only online starting point.** It covers Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800, in Spanish, browse-only (64 images). Access it through the FamilySearch image viewer using that image group number. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Spanish (and French for pre-1763 records) is required.** All colonial-period records at Arkansas Post from 1763–1800 are in Spanish; earlier records are in French. Plan for translation assistance if needed.
- **The Archivo General de Indias (AGI) 'Papeles de Cuba' series is the primary source for Spanish Louisiana civil and military records**, including those from Arkansas Post. The PARES digital portal (http://pares.mcu.es) has digitized portions and is freely searchable. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Contact the Arkansas History Commission before planning a research trip.** They hold transcriptions and some originals and can advise on what has been indexed or published. https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission
- **Check published transcriptions first.** Arkansas colonial records have been partially transcribed in the *Arkansas Historical Quarterly* and in published volumes. Search WorldCat for these before incurring travel costs to Spain or Washington, DC.
- **Search adjoining Louisiana repositories.** The broader administrative jurisdiction for Arkansas Post was New Orleans. If your ancestor passed through or lived in Louisiana before or after residing in Arkansas, records may be found at the Historic New Orleans Collection, the Louisiana State Archives, and the New Orleans Notarial Archives. The neighboring jurisdictions to the south and east (the Red River districts and Natchitoches) also generated records for French and Spanish Louisiana that may name Arkansas settlers.
- **Spanish land grants may have been confirmed by the US after 1803.** Search the BLM GLO records (glorecords.blm.gov) for the US confirmation patent, which may describe the original Spanish grant and name the grantee. ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Arkansas Post is now a National Memorial.** The Arkansas Post National Memorial (National Park Service) has interpretive materials and may point researchers to scholarly resources and bibliographies on the colonial period.
- **DNA evidence.** Given the very sparse documentary record, Y-DNA or autosomal DNA tested against French Creole and Spanish colonial Louisiana surname databases may help bridge gaps when documents cannot.

Here is the locality guide's response:

---

**Ohio circa 1790 — Locality Guide**

Searching for Ohio ancestors around 1790 means searching in the **Northwest Territory**, not the state of Ohio — Ohio did not exist until **1803**. The territory had almost no civil record-keeping infrastructure: there was no registration of births or deaths, and the first county (Washington County, centered on Marietta) was only organized in **1788**, followed by Hamilton County in the southwest in **1790**.

### Key Records Available

The most important records for this era are:

1. **Land Records** — FamilySearch has a 51-image browse-only volume of territorial land records (1788–1799) and an indexed collection of Ohio land records (1787–1840).
2. **Church Records** — FamilySearch holds 678,234 records in its Ohio church records collection (baptisms, burials, marriages).
3. **Revolutionary War Bounty Land Warrant Applications** — Many early settlers came specifically to claim veterans' land. Applications are held at the **National Archives**.
4. **1790 Federal Census** — Nominally covered the territory but had very incomplete coverage.

### Repository Notes

- **County probate and court records** from the territorial era are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus, not widely available online.
- Settlers in the **Virginia Military District** (south-central Ohio, between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) have land warrants at the **Virginia State Library**, not Ohio archives.
- Settlers in the **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio) have records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society** in Cleveland.

### Research Strategy

Identify which of the two early counties — **Washington** or **Hamilton** — held jurisdiction over your ancestor's specific location, then:
1. Search the corresponding courthouse records.
2. Check the Ohio History Connection.
3. Pursue any bounty land warrant applications, which may provide valuable family details.

quirks: In 1790, Ohio was the Northwest Territory — the jurisdiction 'Ohio' did not exist until statehood on March 1, 1803. All records before 1803 are territorial or county records under Northwest Territory authority.

Washington County (organized 1788) was the only county until Hamilton County (organized 1790) — determine which county held jurisdiction over the ancestor's location at the time of each event before searching county-level records.
No civil birth or death registration existed in the Northwest Territory in 1790 — church records are the primary source for vital events during the entire pre-statehood period.
The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) used metes-and-bounds survey; warrants are at the Virginia State Library, not at Ohio archives.
The Connecticut Western Reserve (northeastern Ohio) was surveyed on a different grid; records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland, not a state archive.

The 1790 federal census had incomplete coverage of the Northwest Territory; absence from it does not prove the ancestor was not present — use territorial land records, tax lists, and militia rosters instead.
Early territorial court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus — not solely at county courthouses.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (1787–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County — the first county organized within what is now Ohio — was created in 1788; Hamilton County followed in 1790. Ohio became a state on March 1, 1803, the first state carved from the Northwest Territory. (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio; FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Washington County seat: Marietta (first permanent American settlement, 1788). Hamilton County seat: Cincinnati (from 1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (federal territory, 1787–1803); administered by a federally appointed governor and territorial courts.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence agriculture, fur trade, military provisioning. Many early settlers were Revolutionary War veterans or their heirs receiving bounty land warrants.
- **Ethnic composition:** Primarily Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; Native American tribes (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) remained active throughout the period. (Wikipedia)
- **Religious denominations:** Not specifically named in any tool result for this period.

- **Establish the county first.** Boundary changes were frequent. Determine whether the ancestor's location fell under Washington County (1788) or Hamilton County (1790) at the time of each event. Events before 1788 have no county-level records. (FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Identify the land district.** The Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, and federal rectangular survey areas each have their own repositories and record formats. Where in Ohio the ancestor settled determines where to search. (FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Use church records as your vital record substitute.** No civil births or deaths were recorded in 1790. Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers — searchable through FamilySearch collection 2246917 — are the primary source.
- **Browse the territorial land records volume.** FamilySearch volume 005112233 (Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799) has only 51 images and is 0% name-indexed. Browse it completely — it is short enough to do so.
- **Bounty land warrants are a critical entry point.** Many early Ohio settlers were Revolutionary War veterans or heirs. A warrant application at NARA or Fold3 may name the ancestor and family members.
- **Do not rely on the 1790 census alone.** Coverage of the Northwest Territory was incomplete. Use territorial tax lists, militia rosters, and land entry records to establish or corroborate presence.
- **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki for Ohio directly.** All four wiki_place_page sections and all constructed-URL wiki_read calls for Ohio-specific pages returned generic non-Ohio content in this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy should be consulted directly. The catalog_search tool was also not available in this environment; search the FamilySearch Catalog at familysearch.org/catalog for Ohio microfilm holdings not captured in the indexed collections above.

Locality guide saved as **loc_001** in your project.

---

**California Gold Rush Research (1848–1865)**

California's record landscape from the Gold Rush era is scattered and uneven, for a few reasons worth knowing up front:

- California went from Mexican territory **directly to statehood** in September 1850 — no territorial phase — so county-level record-keeping only began at statehood.
- The **1850 federal census was largely destroyed**. The best early name snapshot is the **1852 California State Census**, which is indexed and widely available.
- Much of the mining population was **male, unmarried, and transient**, leaving very thin paper trails. A negative result online does not mean your ancestor wasn't there.

---

### Key Records and Where to Find Them

| Record Type | What It Captures | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Ship passenger manifests** | Sea arrivals via Cape Horn or Panama | National Archives, San Bruno, CA |
| **1852 California State Census** | First well-preserved population snapshot | Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch |
| **Mining claim registers** | Filed by the miner's county of operation | County Recorder's office for each Mother Lode county |
| **County birth & marriage registers** | From 1850 forward, survival varies | Individual county courthouses |
| **Probate records** | Estate, wills, heirs — very useful for transients who died with property | County courthouse |
| **Diaries, journals & manuscript collections** | Unindexed personal accounts, letters | California State Library; Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) |

---

### Most Useful Repositories

- **National Archives – Pacific Region (San Bruno)**: Federal records, passenger lists, naturalization records.
- **California State Library (Sacramento)**: State census, newspapers, manuscript collections.
- **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley**: One of the largest collections of Gold Rush-era primary sources — diaries, journals, letters, and photographs.
- **California Historical Society (San Francisco)**: Business records, daguerreotypes, mining company papers.
- **County Recorders' Offices**: Mining claims and land records filed at the county where the miner worked. The principal Mother Lode counties include El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Nevada, and Placer counties.

---

### Practical Next Step

Narrow your search to the **specific county** where your ancestor likely mined or settled. That will point you to the right county recorder, probate court, and any surviving local newspapers. The Mother Lode ran through a fairly defined corridor of counties, so knowing a camp or town name (even approximate) goes a long way.
