entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a state on September 9, 1850, following the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848), which transferred the territory from Mexico to the United States. California bypassed territorial status entirely. [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush]
- **Administrative center:** Under US military governance 1848–1850; state capital established at Sacramento by 1854
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Alta California under Mexico until 1848; US military rule 1848–1850; State of California from September 1850
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people migrated to California during the Gold Rush (1848–1855). The 1850 federal census was the first taken as a state, though it was partially destroyed. [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush; California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy]
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, commerce, and service industries grew rapidly alongside mining
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — Americans from all states, Mexicans and Latin Americans, Chinese, French, British, Chilean, Australian, and others, drawn by gold [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush]
- **Religious denominations:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for California Church Records did not return California-specific content in this survey; denomination data is unconfirmed from tool results. Consult the California State Library, Bancroft Library, and California Historical Society.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; statehood September 9, 1850; California State Census 1852; Civil War 1861–1865 (California remained in the Union)

## Boundary changes
- **Before January 1848:** Alta California under Mexican sovereignty; Franciscan Mission records kept 1769–1834/1850
- **January 1848 – September 1850:** US territory under military governance; no territorial legislature; no formal county structure
- **September 9, 1850:** California admitted to the Union; 27 original counties formed, with more added in subsequent years
- Records for 1848–1850 are sparse because formal county government did not exist until statehood; for this window, consult NARA and military records
- The wiki_search result from the California Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy) notes that before American control, California was part of Mexico (and before 1821, Spanish colonial territory)

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level birth and marriage registration is confirmed from 1850 by the FamilySearch collections "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (collection 1452832). Both are at the **county** level. The statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from this survey — the FamilySearch California Vital Records page returned only generic content; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 (789,456 indexed records); county-level marriage records from 1850 (567,890 indexed records). Death registration date range is not confirmed by this survey's tool results.
- **Where held:** County recorder's offices; FamilySearch indexed collections at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276 (births) and https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832 (marriages)
- **Gaps:** The Gold Rush population was predominantly male and highly transient; many miners were unmarried, had no children born in California, and left or died there without generating a county vital record
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal/marriage registers; mining camp records; cemetery inscriptions; overland trail rosters

### Church records
- **Mission records (1769–1850):** Franciscan missions maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1769 through the close of the Mission era. FamilySearch holds 98,765 indexed Mission Records (collection 1804372, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372). These primarily document Native Californian and mestizo populations and are background context for the 1850s period rather than a primary source for Gold Rush migrants.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish and Latin
- **Post-1850 church records:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for California Church Records did not return California-specific content in this survey. Consult the California State Library, the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley, and the California Historical Society for denominational church records from the Gold Rush era.

### Census records
- **California State Census, 1852:** A digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 006601001, 522 images) — 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable. This is the single most important census for Gold Rush research because the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed. [California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy] Digitization level: **indexed + images**.
- **Federal census 1850:** California's first federal census, but partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. [California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy] Digitization level: **indexed + images** for surviving returns (FamilySearch and Ancestry)
- **Federal census 1860:** Covers the full population at the close of the Gold Rush era; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules (listing deaths in the prior year) also exist for 1860.
- **FamilySearch Wiki page for California Census** did not return California-specific content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Census directly for further enumeration details.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Pre-1906 naturalizations (declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization) could be filed in any California court of record.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for the specific county where the miner last resided or held property (i.e., the specific mining county — El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Nevada, Placer, etc.)
- **Access:** Largely physical only; some records may be at the California State Archives on deposit. The FamilySearch Wiki page for California Probate Records did not return California-specific content in this survey.
- **Note:** Gold Rush-era court minutes may document claim disputes, debt actions, and estate proceedings naming individuals who left no other California record.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal (public) land state following statehood; land patents from the General Land Office are available at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal patents issued by the GLO for entries after 1850; Mexican-era land grants (ranchos) were adjudicated by the US Land Commission from 1851, and confirmed grant patents are at NARA San Francisco.
- **Mining claims:** NOT land patents — recorded at county recorders' offices for the county where the claim was located. A digitized browse-only volume of San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 exists at FamilySearch (DGS 006601002, 340 images); it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki page for California Land and Property** did not return California-specific content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War 1846–1848 (service records at NARA); California State Militia (records at California State Archives); Civil War 1861–1865 (service records, pension files, draft records at NARA and Fold3)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (searchable via Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/)

California during the 1848-1865 Gold Rush period produced a surprisingly scattered record landscape. The state went directly from Mexican territory to US statehood in September 1850 with no territorial phase in between, so formal county record-keeping only began at that point, and the 1850 federal census was partially destroyed, leaving the 1852 California State Census as the first well-preserved name-indexed snapshot of who was there. A large portion of the mining population was male, unmarried, and transient, so many men left no California record at all except a mining claim, and a negative result in online databases should not be treated as proof of absence.

The logical next step is to narrow from the state level down to a specific county where your ancestor likely mined or settled, which will point you to the right county recorder, courthouse, and probate records.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a state on September 9, 1850, following the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848), which transferred the territory from Mexico to the United States. California bypassed territorial status entirely. [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush]
- **Administrative center:** Under US military governance 1848–1850; state capital established at Sacramento by 1854
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Alta California under Mexico until 1848; US military rule 1848–1850; State of California from September 1850
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people migrated to California during the Gold Rush (1848–1855). The 1850 federal census was the first taken as a state, though it was partially destroyed. [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush; California Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy]
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, commerce, and service industries grew rapidly alongside mining
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — Americans from all states, Mexicans and Latin Americans, Chinese, French, British, Chilean, Australian, and others, drawn by gold [Wikipedia: California Gold Rush]
- **Religious denominations:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for California Church Records did not return California-specific content in this survey; denomination data is unconfirmed from tool results. Consult the California State Library, Bancroft Library, and California Historical Society.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; statehood September 9, 1850; California State Census 1852; Civil War 1861–1865 (California remained in the Union)

## Boundary changes
- **Before January 1848:** Alta California under Mexican sovereignty; Franciscan Mission records kept 1769–1834/1850
- **January 1848 – September 1850:** US territory under military governance; no territorial legislature; no formal county structure
- **September 9, 1850:** California admitted to the Union; 27 original counties formed, with more added in subsequent years
- Records for 1848–1850 are sparse because formal county government did not exist until statehood; for this window, consult NARA and military records
- The wiki_search result from the California Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy) notes that before American control, California was part of Mexico (and before 1821, Spanish colonial territory)

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level birth and marriage registration is confirmed from 1850 by the FamilySearch collections "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (collection 1452832). Both are at the **county** level. The statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from this survey — the FamilySearch California Vital Records page returned only generic content; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 (789,456 indexed records); county-level marriage records from 1850 (567,890 indexed records). Death registration date range is not confirmed by this survey's tool results.
- **Where held:** County recorder's offices; FamilySearch indexed collections at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276 (births) and https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832 (marriages)
- **Gaps:** The Gold Rush population was predominantly male and highly transient; many miners were unmarried, had no children born in California, and left or died there without generating a county vital record
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal/marriage registers; mining camp records; cemetery inscriptions; overland trail rosters

FamilySearch holds 98,765 indexed Mission Records (collection 1804372, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372). - **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish and Latin
- **Post-1850 church records:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for California Church Records did not return California-specific content in this survey. Here is the locality guide for **New York City in the colonial 1700s** (recorded as **loc_001**):

---

## New York City (Manhattan / New York County), 1700–1783

### Period Overview
This period spans the British colonial era through the Revolutionary War occupation (1776–1783). There is **no civil registration** — churches are the only primary source for births, marriages, and burials.

---

### Key Record Types

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Church registers** (Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Trinity, Presbyterian) | Births, marriages, burials | Primary vital records substitute; some digitized on FamilySearch (1640–1940) |
| **Dutch Reformed registers** (NYC-specific) | 1700–1776 | One digitized volume; **unindexed, must be browsed image by image; in Dutch** |
| **Probate records** (Prerogative Court of New York) | From 1629, indexed | Searchable on FamilySearch |
| **Land records** (conveyances, provincial patents) | Colonial era | Key for property-owning families |
| **Colonial court records** (Mayor's Court) | 1700s | Local civil disputes |
| **Militia rolls & tax assessment lists** | Replace censuses | The first U.S. federal census is not until 1790 |
| **Loyalist records** | 1776–1783 | British occupation disrupted civilian record-keeping; many residents appear in Loyalist files rather than Patriot pension files |

---

### Repositories

- **FamilySearch.org** — NY church records (1640–1940), probate records (indexed from 1629), and digitized Dutch Reformed volume
- **New York State Archives** — Major repository for provincial/colonial records not microfilmed
- **New York City Municipal Archives** — Municipal records
- **New-York Historical Society** — Manuscript collections, maps, and colonial-era documents
- **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** — Compiled records, published abstracts, and finding aids

---

### Important Caveats
- **No federal census before 1790** — use militia rolls and tax lists as substitutes
- **British occupation (1776–1783)** disrupted record-keeping; if ancestors stayed in the city during the war, look for them in Loyalist records
- **Dutch-language records** require either reading Dutch or finding an abstracted translation

---

### Next Step
Consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly for the most current collection listings:
👉 [New York City Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established 1626 (Dutch); seized by English and renamed New York in 1664; by 1700 firmly within the Province of New York under British colonial rule
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial, 1664-1776); State of New York (1776-1783)
- **Population during period:** No tool data was returned for population figures for this place and period; per Wikipedia the city was the most populous urban center in colonial British North America by mid-century
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; Atlantic trade, mercantile commerce, shipbuilding, crafts and artisan trades
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Dutch (substantial Dutch community persisted through the 1700s), French Huguenot, and a smaller number of German, Jewish, and African-descent inhabitants (enslaved and free)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation); Anglican (Church of England — Trinity Church, established 1698); Presbyterian; French Reformed (Huguenot); Lutheran; Jewish (Shearith Israel, oldest Jewish congregation in North America); Quaker
- **Key historical events:** British colonial administration throughout the century; Seven Years' War / French and Indian War (1754-1763); growing pre-Revolutionary tensions from the 1760s; British military occupation of New York City from September 1776 through November 1783 — the entire Revolutionary War period

## Boundary changes
- Through the entire 1700-1783 period, New York City was coterminous with Manhattan Island (New York County). No boundary changes within this target window affected the city proper.
- Before 1776, records were created under the authority of the Province of New York. After independence (1776), the jurisdiction became part of the State of New York — but because the British occupied the city from 1776 to 1783, this administrative transition had limited immediate practical effect on record-keeping in NYC during those years.
- Note: The modern five-borough consolidation did not occur until 1898. Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and Westchester County were all separate jurisdictions in the 1700s.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in colonial New York during the 1700-1783 period. The FamilySearch wiki pages for New York Vital Records resolved to a generic fallback and did not return a specific start date; from context, statewide civil registration in New York did not begin until decades after the colonial era. For this period, church records are the exclusive primary source for vital events.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1700-1783
- **Where held:** Not applicable
- **Gaps:** The entire period lacks civil registration
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records — see Church Records section below. These are the sole primary vital-record substitute.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (congregation present since 1628); Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, chartered 1697); Presbyterian (First Presbyterian Church, founded 1716); French Reformed (Huguenot); Lutheran; Shearith Israel (Jewish, records from 1695)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers this period at the state level
  - 1 digitized volume specifically identified for New York City: imageGroup 007733180 — 211 images, Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 — **browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; language is Dutch**
  - The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society (NYHS) hold extensive colonial church record collections (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
  - Trinity Church (Anglican) records are held by Trinity Church archives in Manhattan
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch and require ability to read 18th-century Dutch script. Anglican and Presbyterian records are in English.
- **Digitization level:** The identified Dutch Reformed volume (007733180) is **browse-only images** — must be examined image by image with no search index. The state-level FamilySearch collection (1469062) is indexed but covers all of New York; coverage within NYC specifically must be verified by searching that collection.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census was taken in 1790 — this falls entirely OUTSIDE the 1700-1783 target period. No federal census records exist for any year within this window.
- **State/provincial census:** No formal decennial census was conducted in colonial New York. Some colonial-era head counts and muster rolls survive but are not equivalent to a census enumeration.
- **Other enumerations:** Provincial militia rolls list men of military age and are a partial substitute for population enumeration (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards and serve a similar locating function.
- **Access:** No digitized, indexed census records exist for 1700-1783.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Testate or intestate:** Those who left wills (testate) had them proved before the Prerogative Court of New York — a provincial-level court, not a county court. Search the Prerogative Court series first. Intestate administration was also handled at the provincial level.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) begins 1629 and fully covers the 1700-1783 window
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; FamilySearch collection 1542780 (indexed + images at state level); the New-York Historical Society published an indexed Abstracts of Wills series covering colonial-era wills (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via FamilySearch collection 1542780; NYHS Abstracts of Wills is a published finding aid (physical and likely available in large library collections)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used British metes-and-bounds descriptions)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the Province of New York, land grants and patents were issued by the colonial governor on behalf of the Crown. The New York State Archives holds the provincial land patent records. The FamilySearch wiki_read for New York Land and Property returned only a generic page — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly for specifics.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds (conveyances), mortgages
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) begins 1630 and fully covers the target period
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk's Office (historic deed books); New York State Archives (provincial patents); FamilySearch collection 2078654 (indexed + images at state level)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via FamilySearch collection 2078654 at state level; city/county deed books may be browse-only in that collection

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713); King George's War (1744-1748); French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754-1763); American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls list men of military age and are a key resource for locating residents (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records); pension files and bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service are at NARA; loyalist claims are at the UK National Archives
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (provincial militia and colonial military records); National Archives and Records Administration — NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for Revolutionary War federal records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Note:** Because NYC was under British occupation 1776-1783, residents who remained were either Loyalists or non-combatants; Patriots who fled the city would have left records in other jurisdictions. Loyalist claims records at the UK National Archives and the New York State Archives are a distinct search track.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, in active use throughout the 1700s); Dutch Reformed church burying grounds; Shearith Israel (Chatham Square Cemetery, one of the oldest Jewish cemeteries in North America)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides some coverage; colonial-era headstones are inconsistently indexed
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual church archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (founded 1725, the first newspaper published continuously in New York) contained news, notices, and some vital event announcements (per Wikipedia)
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper archives; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides some digitized historical newspaper access
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, runaway slave advertisements, ship arrivals — especially useful because vital records are absent

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary Atlantic port of entry for the colonial city
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists; later naturalization records (though formal naturalization courts were less systematized in the colonial period)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger list records; the New-York Historical Society and NYGBS hold colonial-era immigration and settlement records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Provincial tax assessment lists by ward; personal property assessments
- **Date range:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards during the colonial period (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). Note: FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) falls just OUTSIDE the 1700-1783 target period and is not applicable here.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New York City Municipal Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for census records, which do not exist for this period. They establish presence in a ward and give a rough wealth assessment.

### Court records
- **Types:** Mayor's Court of New York City records (civil suits, minor criminal matters); Court of Chancery; Supreme Court of the Province of New York
- **Key content:** The Mayor's Court records are an important source for colonial NYC families, recording commercial disputes, debt actions, and property matters (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Court minutes often record the names of ordinary residents as witnesses, jurors, or parties.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New York City Municipal Archives
- **Digitization level:** These records are primarily physical only or available through archives on-site; digitization coverage is limited.

### Other record types
- **Colonial manuscripts:** The New York Colonial Manuscripts held at the New York State Archives document provincial governance, land transactions, and administrative matters — a primary source for the 1700-1776 period (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **City directories:** City directories for NYC begin in the late 1780s (just after the target period); the earliest editions can place families in the city immediately following the Revolution
- **Local and published histories:** 19th-century published histories of New York City frequently reprint colonial records, transcribe early church registers, and carry biographical sketches of founding families

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (coll. 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (coll. 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (coll. 1542780) | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including colonial-era militia | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New York Gazette | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery and burial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War service and pension records; passenger lists | Free / fee for copies |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (begins 1790, outside target period) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching New York City 1700-1783 (no nextPageToken — this is the complete set). The broader New York state-level collections_search returned 5 collections; 3 overlap the target period (church, land, probate). This represents all that volume_search and collections_search found; there are almost certainly additional microfilmed and physical-only record sets not captured here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | Provincial colonial manuscripts, militia rolls, court records, land patents | In-person; some records available on microfilm |
| New York City Municipal Archives | City administrative records, early vital records | In-person; some online |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Extensive colonial-era collections, transcriptions, published finding aids | In-person; some online via subscription |

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established 1626 (Dutch); seized by English and renamed New York in 1664; by 1700 firmly within the Province of New York under British colonial rule
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial, 1664-1776); State of New York (1776-1783)
- **Population during period:** No tool data was returned for population figures for this place and period; per Wikipedia the city was the most populous urban center in colonial British North America by mid-century
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; Atlantic trade, mercantile commerce, shipbuilding, crafts and artisan trades
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Dutch (substantial Dutch community persisted through the 1700s), French Huguenot, and a smaller number of German, Jewish, and African-descent inhabitants (enslaved and free)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation); Anglican (Church of England — Trinity Church, established 1698); Presbyterian; French Reformed (Huguenot); Lutheran; Jewish (Shearith Israel, oldest Jewish congregation in North America); Quaker
- **Key historical events:** British colonial administration throughout the century; Seven Years' War / French and Indian War (1754-1763); growing pre-Revolutionary tensions from the 1760s; British military occupation of New York City from September 1776 through November 1783 — the entire Revolutionary War period

## Boundary changes
- Through the entire 1700-1783 period, New York City was coterminous with Manhattan Island (New York County). No boundary changes within this target window affected the city proper.
- Before 1776, records were created under the authority of the Province of New York. After independence (1776), the jurisdiction became part of the State of New York — but because the British occupied the city from 1776 to 1783, this administrative transition had limited immediate practical effect on record-keeping in NYC during those years.
- Note: The modern five-borough consolidation did not occur until 1898. Kings County (Brooklyn), Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and Westchester County were all separate jurisdictions in the 1700s.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in colonial New York during the 1700-1783 period. The FamilySearch wiki pages for New York Vital Records resolved to a generic fallback and did not return a specific start date; from context, statewide civil registration in New York did not begin until decades after the colonial era. For this period, church records are the exclusive primary source for vital events.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1700-1783
- **Where held:** Not applicable
- **Gaps:** The entire period lacks civil registration
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records — see Church Records section below. These are the sole primary vital-record substitute.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (congregation present since 1628); Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, chartered 1697); Presbyterian (First Presbyterian Church, founded 1716); French Reformed (Huguenot); Lutheran; Shearith Israel (Jewish, records from 1695)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers this period at the state level
  - 1 digitized volume specifically identified for New York City: imageGroup 007733180 — 211 images, Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 — **browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; language is Dutch**
  - The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society (NYHS) hold extensive colonial church record collections (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
  - Trinity Church (Anglican) records are held by Trinity Church archives in Manhattan
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch and require ability to read 18th-century Dutch script. Anglican and Presbyterian records are in English.
- **Digitization level:** The identified Dutch Reformed volume (007733180) is **browse-only images** — must be examined image by image with no search index. The state-level FamilySearch collection (1469062) is indexed but covers all of New York; coverage within NYC specifically must be verified by searching that collection.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census was taken in 1790 — this falls entirely OUTSIDE the 1700-1783 target period. No federal census records exist for any year within this window.
- **State/provincial census:** No formal decennial census was conducted in colonial New York. Some colonial-era head counts and muster rolls survive but are not equivalent to a census enumeration.
- **Other enumerations:** Provincial militia rolls list men of military age and are a partial substitute for population enumeration (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards and serve a similar locating function.
- **Access:** No digitized, indexed census records exist for 1700-1783.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Testate or intestate:** Those who left wills (testate) had them proved before the Prerogative Court of New York — a provincial-level court, not a county court. Search the Prerogative Court series first. Intestate administration was also handled at the provincial level.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) begins 1629 and fully covers the 1700-1783 window
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; FamilySearch collection 1542780 (indexed + images at state level); the New-York Historical Society published an indexed Abstracts of Wills series covering colonial-era wills (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via FamilySearch collection 1542780; NYHS Abstracts of Wills is a published finding aid (physical and likely available in large library collections)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used British metes-and-bounds descriptions)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the Province of New York, land grants and patents were issued by the colonial governor on behalf of the Crown. The New York State Archives holds the provincial land patent records. The FamilySearch wiki_read for New York Land and Property returned only a generic page — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly for specifics.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds (conveyances), mortgages
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) begins 1630 and fully covers the target period
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk's Office (historic deed books); New York State Archives (provincial patents); FamilySearch collection 2078654 (indexed + images at state level)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via FamilySearch collection 2078654 at state level; city/county deed books may be browse-only in that collection

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713); King George's War (1744-1748); French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754-1763); American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls list men of military age and are a key resource for locating residents (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records); pension files and bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service are at NARA; loyalist claims are at the UK National Archives
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (provincial militia and colonial military records); National Archives and Records Administration — NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for Revolutionary War federal records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Note:** Because NYC was under British occupation 1776-1783, residents who remained were either Loyalists or non-combatants; Patriots who fled the city would have left records in other jurisdictions. Loyalist claims records at the UK National Archives and the New York State Archives are a distinct search track.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, in active use throughout the 1700s); Dutch Reformed church burying grounds; Shearith Israel (Chatham Square Cemetery, one of the oldest Jewish cemeteries in North America)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides some coverage; colonial-era headstones are inconsistently indexed
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual church archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (founded 1725, the first newspaper published continuously in New York) contained news, notices, and some vital event announcements (per Wikipedia)
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper archives; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides some digitized historical newspaper access
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, runaway slave advertisements, ship arrivals — especially useful because vital records are absent

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary Atlantic port of entry for the colonial city
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists; later naturalization records (though formal naturalization courts were less systematized in the colonial period)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger list records; the New-York Historical Society and NYGBS hold colonial-era immigration and settlement records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Provincial tax assessment lists by ward; personal property assessments
- **Date range:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards during the colonial period (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). Note: FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432) falls just OUTSIDE the 1700-1783 target period and is not applicable here.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New York City Municipal Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for census records, which do not exist for this period. They establish presence in a ward and give a rough wealth assessment.

### Court records
- **Types:** Mayor's Court of New York City records (civil suits, minor criminal matters); Court of Chancery; Supreme Court of the Province of New York
- **Key content:** The Mayor's Court records are an important source for colonial NYC families, recording commercial disputes, debt actions, and property matters (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Court minutes often record the names of ordinary residents as witnesses, jurors, or parties.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; New York City Municipal Archives
- **Digitization level:** These records are primarily physical only or available through archives on-site; digitization coverage is limited.

### Other record types
- **Colonial manuscripts:** The New York Colonial Manuscripts held at the New York State Archives document provincial governance, land transactions, and administrative matters — a primary source for the 1700-1776 period (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **City directories:** City directories for NYC begin in the late 1780s (just after the target period); the earliest editions can place families in the city immediately following the Revolution
- **Local and published histories:** 19th-century published histories of New York City frequently reprint colonial records, transcribe early church registers, and carry biographical sketches of founding families

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (coll. 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (coll. 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (coll. 1542780) | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including colonial-era militia | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New York Gazette | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery and burial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War service and pension records; passenger lists | Free / fee for copies |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (begins 1790, outside target period) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume matching New York City 1700-1783 (no nextPageToken — this is the complete set). The broader New York state-level collections_search returned 5 collections; 3 overlap the target period (church, land, probate). This represents all that volume_search and collections_search found; there are almost certainly additional microfilmed and physical-only record sets not captured here.

### Physical repositories

| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Extensive colonial-era collections, transcriptions, published finding aids | In-person; some online via subscription |
| New-York Historical Society (NYHS) | Colonial manuscripts, published Abstracts of Wills, church record transcriptions | In-person; some online |

| Shearith Israel Archives | Jewish congregation records from 1695 | Contact congregation directly |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it achieved formal U.S. statehood in 1788. During 1775–1783 it operated as the Commonwealth of Virginia under a new state constitution adopted in 1776.
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital through 1779), then Richmond (from 1780)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** None during this period — Virginia functioned as an independent commonwealth
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period; no confirmed figures are available from this survey.
- **Economy:** Tobacco agriculture, grist mills, iron works, maritime trade, frontier settlement
- **Ethnic composition:** Primarily English-descended colonists; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley and western frontier; enslaved Africans formed a large portion of the eastern (Tidewater and Piedmont) population
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (the established church until disestablishment during the Revolution); Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, and Lutheran congregations particularly in western counties
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia). British raids along the Tidewater coast throughout the war; Cornwallis's campaign through Virginia in 1781; Battle of Yorktown (1781), the decisive engagement ending the war.

## Boundary changes

Virginia's external boundaries were essentially stable during 1775–1783, but its internal county structure changed constantly as western settlement expanded. Kentucky County (carved from Fincastle County in 1776) and subsequent Kentucky-area counties remained under Virginia jurisdiction throughout this period — Kentucky did not become a separate state until 1792. place_search_all returned no historical boundary records for Virginia in this session, so no further subdivision dates can be confirmed from tool results. Researchers tracing families in far western Virginia should check Virginia-era Kentucky county records (Fayette, Jefferson, and Lincoln counties formed from Kentucky County in 1780), as those records were created while those places were still Virginia jurisdiction.

## Available record types

All record-keeping during 1775–1783 operated at the county and parish level. No statewide civil vital registration existed. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records, Military Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, and Census all returned only generic content in this session — Virginia-specific details below come from wiki_search results and FamilySearch collection and volume data.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content in this session; no Virginia-specific civil registration start date can be cited from tool results. No statewide birth, marriage, or death registration was in effect during 1775–1783.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and marriage registers were kept at the county courthouse. Births and deaths were not systematically registered.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia (Richmond) holds many series. FamilySearch collection 1734285 ("Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900") includes marriage records.
- **Gaps:** No statewide vital registration; births and deaths before civil registration are not systematically documented.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and county marriage bonds are the primary vital record sources for this period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Church of England (established church, parish records widespread throughout Tidewater and Piedmont); Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, and German Lutheran congregations present especially in western counties.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry books (which include poor relief records naming ordinary residents).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 ("Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929," 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images). Vestry books and parish registers also held at the Library of Virginia and denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Church Records page returned only generic content in this session. Consult the Library of Virginia's online catalog for parish-specific holdings.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) would have captured Revolutionary War veterans and families, but it was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. No federal census was conducted during 1775–1783. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State enumerations:** Virginia conducted personal property tax enumerations beginning in 1782. FamilySearch holds digitized volume 005301449 (Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images). This volume is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — it must be searched by text string, not by name field.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection 1456723, 456,789 records) also covers this series.
- **Access:** Volume 005301449 — full-text searchable, not name-indexed (browse/text search required).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, inventories, administrations, guardianships, county court order books.
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts operated continuously from the colonial period. Wartime actions in court order books include soldiers' estates, orphan guardianships, and locally administered militia affairs.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 2134567 ("Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920," 1,789,012 records). FamilySearch also holds a partially indexed digitized volume of county court order books for Augusta County, Virginia, 1775–1795 (volume 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed + images for the indexed portion). Collection 1734285 ("Land, Marriage, and Will Records") includes will and probate entries.
- **Note:** Whether an estate was testate (will present) or intestate (no will) determines which probate series to search — wills vs. administration bonds and inventories.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; land was granted from the colonial governor's office and, after 1776, from the Commonwealth's Land Office — not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content in this session. Virginia land grants and patents were issued by the Commonwealth's Land Office; the Library of Virginia holds these records.
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deeds, bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service.
- **Revolutionary War bounty lands:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to their grants are held at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch holds digitized volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, Virginia, 1779–1800, 341 images) — browse-only: 0% name-indexed and NOT full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Where held:** County courthouses for deeds; Library of Virginia for state grants and patents; FamilySearch collection 1734285.

### Military records — PRIMARY FOCUS

This is the richest and most concentrated record class for the 1775–1783 period.

**FamilySearch:**
- Collection 1945678: "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (345,678 records, 172,839 images) — searchable on FamilySearch.
- Volume 005301447: Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, Virginia, 1779–1800 (341 images) — browse-only; 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.

**National Archives (NARA):**
- Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15. These files often include wives' and children's affidavits naming parents, siblings, marriage dates, and places — among the most genealogically detailed sources for this period.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Library of Virginia (Richmond):**
- Virginia militia records (distinct from the Continental Line) are held at the Library of Virginia.
- Warrant and survey records for the Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty lands.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Virginia State Navy:**
- Virginia maintained its own State Navy; records are a distinct series named in the FamilySearch Wiki. Likely held at the Library of Virginia; online access status not confirmed by tool results.

**Fold3:** Fold3 (subscription) is a curated external resource returned by this survey; it holds digitized NARA military collections including Revolutionary War pension files and service records.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) is among the curated external resources returned by this survey. Coverage of pre-1800 Virginia cemeteries varies widely; many rural and plantation burial grounds were not formally recorded.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records for this period are rare. DAR transcription projects and local genealogical society records are the primary compiled sources.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Virginia's colonial newspapers included multiple editions of the Virginia Gazette, which carried military notices, estate advertisements, and political news during this period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, curated external resource returned by this survey); Library of Virginia holds microfilm of the Virginia Gazette.
- **Content value:** Runaway notices, estate settlements, sheriff's sales, and military-related public notices are particularly useful.

### Immigration/emigration records

Formal immigration records did not exist during this period; naturalization became a federal process only in 1790. Arriving families appear in county court records or church registers rather than passenger manifests. Post-war emigration from Virginia — particularly westward migration to Kentucky — is documented through county deed releases, estate closings, and Kentucky-area county records beginning after 1780. Kentucky was still Virginia's jurisdiction through 1791, so early Kentucky records (Fayette, Jefferson, Lincoln counties) are Virginia records.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists, personal property tax lists from 1782), land tax.
- **Date range:** Virginia personal property tax records begin 1782 — the earliest statewide enumeration of taxable persons, and the principal substitute for the destroyed 1790 federal census.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1456723 ("Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850," 456,789 records); FamilySearch volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed).
- **Substitute value:** Personal property tax lists and land tax lists from 1782 onward are indispensable for Revolutionary War-era research — they are often the only annual record placing a person in a specific county during and immediately after the war years.

### Other record types

- **Loyalist records:** County court proceedings against loyalists appear in county order books. Loyalist claims filed with the British Loyalist Claims Commission (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK) may name Virginia families who remained loyal to the Crown.
- **Pension files:** NARA RG 15 pension application files are among the richest genealogical sources of the period. Pension applications filed by veterans, widows, and heirs contain affidavits identifying parents, siblings, marriage dates, and places.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1945678 (Military Records 1775-1783); 1598230 (Church Records 1680-1929); 1734285 (Land, Marriage, Will 1600-1900); 1456723 (Tax Records 1782-1850); 2134567 (County Court Records 1650-1920) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files, service records (NARA digitizations) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census and other collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids; some online ordering for records | Free / fee varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 3 digitized volumes for Virginia 1775–1800 with no nextPageToken — this is the complete volume set returned by the query.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Militia records; bounty land warrants; land grants and patents; personal property tax lists; vestry books; colonial court records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some records digitized |
| National Archives (NARA) | RG 93 (Continental Line service records, muster rolls); RG 15 (pension and bounty-land warrant files) | In-person at College Park, MD; Fold3 digitizations; NARA online order system |
| Virginia county courthouses | Deed books, court order books, will books, marriage bonds | In-person; many series microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Denominational archives | Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker congregation records | Varies by denomination; contact denominational headquarters |
| The National Archives (UK), Kew | British Loyalist Claims Commission files | In-person or online catalog (Discovery) |

## Records NOT online

- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia — digitization status not confirmed by tool results; may require in-person or correspondence access.
- Virginia State Navy records — named in the FamilySearch Wiki result but online access status not confirmed by tool results.
- County marriage bonds and registers not included in FamilySearch collection 1734285 — physical courthouse access or Library of Virginia.
- Loyalist Claims Commission files — The National Archives (UK); not freely digitized.
- Most colonial Anglican/Episcopal vestry books not covered by FamilySearch collection 1598230.
- FamilySearch volume 005301447 (bounty land warrants, 341 images) is online but must be browsed image by image with no name index or full-text search.

## Known record losses

- **1790 Federal Census for Virginia destroyed:** The 1790 federal census, which would have been the first post-war enumeration capturing Revolutionary War veterans and their households, was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Virginia's 1782–1784 personal property tax lists are the principal substitute. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **County courthouse losses:** Individual Virginia courthouses have suffered fires and other losses at various points in history. The extent of losses varies by county and is not catalogued by tool results for this session. Researchers should check the Library of Virginia's county-by-county records inventory before assuming a county's holdings are complete.

## Research tips

- **Start with military records, then follow the pension trail.** Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia). NARA RG 15 pension application files are the genealogically richest sources: wives and children filed affidavits naming parents, siblings, marriage places, and dates. Check both RG 93 (Continental Line) and militia records at the Library of Virginia — a soldier may appear in both series. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Use 1782–1786 personal property tax lists as your primary census substitute.** Virginia's personal property tax began in 1782 and provides an annual head-of-household listing by county. FamilySearch collection 1456723 and digitized volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) are starting points. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Trace bounty land warrants to locate post-war settlement.** Virginia's grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (warrant records at the Library of Virginia; FamilySearch volume 005301447, browse-only) link a veteran's service to his later land settlement — essential for families who migrated to Ohio or Kentucky.
- **County court order books capture wartime community life.** Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images, 61% indexed on FamilySearch) illustrates the kind of material available: orphan guardianships, estates of soldiers, county-administered militia affairs, and road maintenance assignments that name ordinary residents.
- **Virginia's county structure was changing during this period.** Several new counties formed from older ones during 1775–1783. Always identify the county as it was constituted at the exact date of the event you're researching, not as it is today. Kentucky-area counties were Virginia jurisdiction through 1791.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content in this session.** The jurisdiction-specific pages for Virginia Vital Records, Military Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, and Census, as well as all four wiki_place_page sections, returned generic fallback content. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for the complete Virginia research wiki.

- **Access:** Volume 005301449 — full-text searchable, not name-indexed (browse/text search required).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, inventories, administrations, guardianships, county court order books.
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts operated continuously from the colonial period. Wartime actions in court order books include soldiers' estates, orphan guardianships, and locally administered militia affairs.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 2134567 ("Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920," 1,789,012 records). FamilySearch also holds a partially indexed digitized volume of county court order books for Augusta County, Virginia, 1775–1795 (volume 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed + images for the indexed portion). Collection 1734285 ("Land, Marriage, and Will Records") includes will and probate entries.
- **Note:** Whether an estate was testate (will present) or intestate (no will) determines which probate series to search — wills vs. administration bonds and inventories.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; land was granted from the colonial governor's office and, after 1776, from the Commonwealth's Land Office — not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Land and Property page returned only generic content in this session. Virginia land grants and patents were issued by the Commonwealth's Land Office; the Library of Virginia holds these records.
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deeds, bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service.
- **Revolutionary War bounty lands:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to their grants are held at the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch holds digitized volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, Virginia, 1779–1800, 341 images) — browse-only: 0% name-indexed and NOT full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Where held:** County courthouses for deeds; Library of Virginia for state grants and patents; FamilySearch collection 1734285.

### Military records — PRIMARY FOCUS

This is the richest and most concentrated record class for the 1775–1783 period.

**FamilySearch:**
- Collection 1945678: "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (345,678 records, 172,839 images) — searchable on FamilySearch.
- Volume 005301447: Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, Virginia, 1779–1800 (341 images) — browse-only; 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.

**National Archives (NARA):**
- Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15. These files often include wives' and children's affidavits naming parents, siblings, marriage dates, and places — among the most genealogically detailed sources for this period.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Library of Virginia (Richmond):**
- Virginia militia records (distinct from the Continental Line) are held at the Library of Virginia.
- Warrant and survey records for the Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty lands.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Virginia State Navy:**
- Virginia maintained its own State Navy; records are a distinct series named in the FamilySearch Wiki. Likely held at the Library of Virginia; online access status not confirmed by tool results.

**Fold3:** Fold3 (subscription) is a curated external resource returned by this survey; it holds digitized NARA military collections including Revolutionary War pension files and service records.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) is among the curated external resources returned by this survey. Coverage of pre-1800 Virginia cemeteries varies widely; many rural and plantation burial grounds were not formally recorded.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records for this period are rare. DAR transcription projects and local genealogical society records are the primary compiled sources.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Virginia's colonial newspapers included multiple editions of the Virginia Gazette, which carried military notices, estate advertisements, and political news during this period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, curated external resource returned by this survey); Library of Virginia holds microfilm of the Virginia Gazette.
- **Content value:** Runaway notices, estate settlements, sheriff's sales, and military-related public notices are particularly useful.

### Immigration/emigration records

Formal immigration records did not exist during this period; naturalization became a federal process only in 1790. Arriving families appear in county court records or church registers rather than passenger manifests. Post-war emigration from Virginia — particularly westward migration to Kentucky — is documented through county deed releases, estate closings, and Kentucky-area county records beginning after 1780. Kentucky was still Virginia's jurisdiction through 1791, so early Kentucky records (Fayette, Jefferson, Lincoln counties) are Virginia records.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists, personal property tax lists from 1782), land tax.
- **Date range:** Virginia personal property tax records begin 1782 — the earliest statewide enumeration of taxable persons, and the principal substitute for the destroyed 1790 federal census.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1456723 ("Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850," 456,789 records); FamilySearch volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed).
- **Substitute value:** Personal property tax lists and land tax lists from 1782 onward are indispensable for Revolutionary War-era research — they are often the only annual record placing a person in a specific county during and immediately after the war years.

### Other record types

- **Loyalist records:** County court proceedings against loyalists appear in county order books. Loyalist claims filed with the British Loyalist Claims Commission (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK) may name Virginia families who remained loyal to the Crown.
- **Pension files:** NARA RG 15 pension application files are among the richest genealogical sources of the period. Pension applications filed by veterans, widows, and heirs contain affidavits identifying parents, siblings, marriage dates, and places.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1945678 (Military Records 1775-1783); 1598230 (Church Records 1680-1929); 1734285 (Land, Marriage, Will 1600-1900); 1456723 (Tax Records 1782-1850); 2134567 (County Court Records 1650-1920) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files, service records (NARA digitizations) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census and other collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids; some online ordering for records | Free / fee varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 3 digitized volumes for Virginia 1775–1800 with no nextPageToken — this is the complete volume set returned by the query.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Militia records; bounty land warrants; land grants and patents; personal property tax lists; vestry books; colonial court records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some records digitized |
| National Archives (NARA) | RG 93 (Continental Line service records, muster rolls); RG 15 (pension and bounty-land warrant files) | In-person at College Park, MD; Fold3 digitizations; NARA online order system |
| Virginia county courthouses | Deed books, court order books, will books, marriage bonds | In-person; many series microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Denominational archives | Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker congregation records | Varies by denomination; contact denominational headquarters |
| The National Archives (UK), Kew | British Loyalist Claims Commission files | In-person or online catalog (Discovery) |

## Records NOT online

- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia — digitization status not confirmed by tool results; may require in-person or correspondence access.
- Virginia State Navy records — named in the FamilySearch Wiki result but online access status not confirmed by tool results.
- County marriage bonds and registers not included in FamilySearch collection 1734285 — physical courthouse access or Library of Virginia.
- Loyalist Claims Commission files — The National Archives (UK); not freely digitized.
- Most colonial Anglican/Episcopal vestry books not covered by FamilySearch collection 1598230.
- FamilySearch volume 005301447 (bounty land warrants, 341 images) is online but must be browsed image by image with no name index or full-text search.

## Known record losses

- **1790 Federal Census for Virginia destroyed:** The 1790 federal census, which would have been the first post-war enumeration capturing Revolutionary War veterans and their households, was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Virginia's 1782–1784 personal property tax lists are the principal substitute. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **County courthouse losses:** Individual Virginia courthouses have suffered fires and other losses at various points in history. The extent of losses varies by county and is not catalogued by tool results for this session. Researchers should check the Library of Virginia's county-by-county records inventory before assuming a county's holdings are complete.

## Research tips

- **Start with military records, then follow the pension trail.** Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia). NARA RG 15 pension application files are the genealogically richest sources: wives and children filed affidavits naming parents, siblings, marriage places, and dates. Check both RG 93 (Continental Line) and militia records at the Library of Virginia — a soldier may appear in both series. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Use 1782–1786 personal property tax lists as your primary census substitute.** Virginia's personal property tax began in 1782 and provides an annual head-of-household listing by county. FamilySearch collection 1456723 and digitized volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed) are starting points. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Trace bounty land warrants to locate post-war settlement.** Virginia's grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (warrant records at the Library of Virginia; FamilySearch volume 005301447, browse-only) link a veteran's service to his later land settlement — essential for families who migrated to Ohio or Kentucky.
- **County court order books capture wartime community life.** Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images, 61% indexed on FamilySearch) illustrates the kind of material available: orphan guardianships, estates of soldiers, county-administered militia affairs, and road maintenance assignments that name ordinary residents.
- **Virginia's county structure was changing during this period.** Several new counties formed from older ones during 1775–1783. Always identify the county as it was constituted at the exact date of the event you're researching, not as it is today. Kentucky-area counties were Virginia jurisdiction through 1791.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content in this session.** The jurisdiction-specific pages for Virginia Vital Records, Military Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, and Census, as well as all four wiki_place_page sections, returned generic fallback content. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for the complete Virginia research wiki.

Here is what the locality guide found for New Orleans, early 1800s research:

---

**Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish, Louisiana), 1800–1860**

### Disaster Context — What Was Lost and When

The single most important fact for this place is that **two catastrophic fires — in 1788 and in 1794 — destroyed most of the colonial city and many of its records before 1800**. This means that even when researching the early 1800s, you should expect gaps that trace back to those colonial-era losses. The fires pre-date most of the target period, so they explain why the documentary record effectively "starts over" around the time of the Louisiana Purchase (1803).

---

### What Survived and Where to Find It

**1. St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers (Births, Marriages, Deaths)**
The primary substitute for vital records lost in the fires is the **sacramental register series of St. Louis Cathedral**, which is the main survival for births, marriages, and deaths in the early 1800s. These registers are organized in **three separate series**:
- White parishioners
- Free people of color
- Enslaved persons

Originals are held by the **Archdiocese of New Orleans**. A portion is available through **FamilySearch**.

**2. New Orleans Notarial Archives**
Because Louisiana follows a **French-derived civil law system** (not English common law), notarial acts are the most important legal record type. These cover land sales, contracts, wills, manumissions, and more — often supplying details found in vital records elsewhere. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages** of acts dating to 1734. However, only a small fraction (167 images, 1803–1820) are digitized on FamilySearch, and those are in French and English with no name index and must be browsed page-by-page. **Most notarial research requires visiting or writing the archive directly.**

**3. FamilySearch Indexed Collections (State Level)**
Four indexed collections at the Louisiana state level overlap the early 1800s:
- Church records
- Parish marriages
- Probate records
- Death index

---

### Recommended Starting Strategy

1. **Begin with St. Louis Cathedral church records** for vital events (births, marriages, deaths).
2. **Then move to notarial acts** for legal and property connections — especially useful for tracing free people of color, manumissions, and family property transfers.
3. Consult the **FamilySearch Research Wiki** directly for current Louisiana locality guidance, as the standard wiki pages returned only generic content during this survey.
