output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide for researching Philadelphia families during the 1793 yellow fever epidemic:

---

**Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic**

Philadelphia in 1793 had no government system for registering births, marriages, or deaths — every record of who died in the epidemic comes from **church burial registers**. Two denominations are especially important:

- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal)
- **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' Church** (Lutheran)

### Epidemic-Specific Sources
These unique sources name victims directly, and are held in manuscript at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**:

- **Mathew Carey's published account** — lists the dead by name
- **Minutes of the citizens' relief committee** — documents aid recipients
- **Bush Hill hospital patient records** — the epidemic's main treatment facility

### Census Records
The **1790 and 1800 federal censuses** (both indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch) can anchor who was in the city before and after the outbreak, helping you identify families who disappeared — likely victims.

### Probate & Estate Records
Because roughly one-tenth of Philadelphia's population died in just a few months, the **county probate court** was flooded with estate and guardianship filings in late 1793 and early 1794. These records exist on FamilySearch but must be **browsed page by page** — there is no name index.

### Important Jurisdictional Caution
Before 1854, the city and surrounding county were **separate governments**. A family living just outside the city proper had records filed under district names like **Northern Liberties** or **Southwark**, not "Philadelphia." Always check which political district your ancestors lived in.

---

**Recommended Next Step:** Identify which church your family attended, then locate and browse that denomination's burial register for the **August–November 1793** window alongside Mathew Carey's published list of the dead.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1682 by William Penn; Philadelphia County and the City of Philadelphia were established at founding. Both place_search entries date to +1682.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 (city, 1793) — source: FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) and Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). The place_population tool returned no data for this period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; commerce, shipping, crafts, professions, early manufacturing, government (national capital 1790–1800)
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding community; German, Scots-Irish, Welsh, Irish, and other immigrant groups; free Black community; small enslaved population (Pennsylvania's 1780 Gradual Abolition Act was in effect)
- **Religious denominations:** Quaker (Society of Friends), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Catholic, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' Church), Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic, August–November 1793, killed approximately 5,000 residents — roughly one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled the city. Mayor Matthew Clarkson coordinated relief; physician Benjamin Rush was prominent in treatment. Sources: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793) and FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1854:** The City of Philadelphia and Philadelphia County were distinct jurisdictions. In 1793 the city proper occupied a relatively small area along the Delaware River; the county included numerous surrounding townships and districts — Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, Moyamensing, Germantown. Records may be filed under these district names.
- **1854:** The Act of Consolidation merged the city and county into one government. Records created before 1854 are under pre-consolidation units.
- **Epidemic period:** County outer boundaries were stable; no county-level splits occurred around 1793.

## Available record types

Note on registration level for this period: The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Probate Records, and Land and Property all returned only the generic fallback page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) in this survey. Registration dates and levels below are drawn from the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records and are cited accordingly; the generic pages do not supply place-specific dates.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793 at any level — city, county, or state. Per the FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records), church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania vital records returned only generic content and do not state a pre-1906 registration date for Pennsylvania or Philadelphia.
- **What exists:** No state-mandated civil birth, marriage, or death registration for 1793. FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (id: 2255317) begins well after the epidemic period and is not applicable.
- **Where held:** N/A for 1793
- **Gaps:** Vital registration is the structural gap for the epidemic period; all individual death recording was done through churches.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial, baptism, and marriage registers; epidemic-specific sources (see below)

### Yellow Fever Epidemic–specific sources (1793)
These sources are unique to the outbreak and are the most direct route to individuals who died or were affected. All sourced from the FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) and Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793):

- **Mathew Carey's published account:** "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" includes a list of names of those who died. A published source available in research libraries and in digitized form online.
- **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports:** The citizens' relief committee maintained minutes and reports naming victims, relief recipients, and officers. Manuscript copies held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Bush Hill served as the main treatment facility. Patient records held by the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Mayor Clarkson's account and Benjamin Rush's records:** These officials left detailed accounts. Benjamin Rush's papers are held at the Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Catholic, Swedish Lutheran. Per the FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records), the city's diverse religious communities each maintained registers, and many colonial and early national registers have been transcribed and published.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Named sources for the epidemic:** Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church) are specifically named as holding burial records from the epidemic period — source: FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- **Indexes:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records — source: FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Where held:** Original registers at individual parishes and denominational archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many; the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds transcribed and published registers.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** 1 volume found via volume_search — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber: 001188322, 145 images). Quaker meeting records. Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Language:** English for most records; Latin for some Catholic registers

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses bracket the epidemic. The generic FamilySearch wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) confirms federal census enumerations ran decennially from 1790. Both censuses cover Philadelphia County. The 1790 census recorded heads of household with household counts (not all members by name); the 1800 census is similar.
- **Access:** U.S. Federal Census Collection available on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results. Both censuses are indexed.
- **Mortality schedules:** The generic FamilySearch wiki page notes mortality schedules ran 1850–1885. These postdate the epidemic; no mortality schedule exists for 1793.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census confirmed for the 1793 period in the returned tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; filed at the county level with the Register of Wills (Philadelphia County Orphans' Court)
- **Epidemic relevance:** The August–November 1793 epidemic killed roughly one-tenth of Philadelphia's population. Expect a significant spike in probate filings in late 1793 and 1794 as estates of epidemic victims were administered and guardians appointed for orphaned children. Search for filings specifically in the 1793–1795 window.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Victims who left wills generate will and probate files (testate); those who died without wills generate administration files (intestate) — search both series.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (id: 1999196) — 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records. Browse-only; must be examined image by image. URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The generic wiki_read page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) confirms county courthouses hold deed books. The FamilySearch wiki page for Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property returned only generic content; specific grant/patent office details are not confirmed from that page.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, patents
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County deed records from 1682 forward
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Philadelphia Register of Deeds hold deed books. Pennsylvania State Archives holds original land grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War ended in 1783 — roughly a decade before the epidemic. Veterans in Philadelphia families may have pension and bounty land warrant files. The War of 1812 is about two decades ahead.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files, bounty land warrants, service records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results. Military records also available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results.
- **Digitization level:** NARA pension files indexed and available via Fold3 (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei churchyard, St. Peter's Churchyard, and numerous other denominational burial grounds; epidemic victims are interred across these sites
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results; many Philadelphia headstones are indexed there
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held at individual churches and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; epidemic-specific burials are in church registers named above (Christ Church, Gloria Dei)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had multiple newspapers in 1793 (including the General Advertiser and others). Death notices and epidemic victim lists appeared in these papers.
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results (subscription). The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Free Library of Philadelphia also hold newspaper collections.
- **Content value:** Death notices, epidemic victim lists, notices of orphaned children, estate settlement notices, public health announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Pre-1820 passenger lists are less detailed than later records but do exist.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization records (filed in any court of record before 1906)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — confirmed in external_links_search results; Ancestry.com also holds digitized passenger records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children. When researching a Philadelphia family with immigrant origins, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County property tax and personal property assessment records
- **Date range:** Assessment records exist from the colonial period through the early national period
- **Substitute value:** Tax records from 1792–1793 can establish a household's presence and economic status just before the epidemic; assessments from 1794–1795 may document property changes from deaths
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds some transcriptions

### Other record types
- **Guardianship records:** With many parents dying in the epidemic, guardianship filings in the Philadelphia Orphans' Court spiked in late 1793–1794. Guardianship files are included in Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196), browse-only.
- **Almshouse and poor relief records:** The Committee appointed by citizens maintained relief records naming recipients; the Philadelphia Almshouse also kept records. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Quaker meeting records:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, browse-only). Quakers were prominent in epidemic relief efforts and documented deaths within their community.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century histories of Philadelphia often reprint early records, list founding families, and narrate the 1793 epidemic by name.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196; 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (id: 1571957; 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (id: 1502909; 198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322; 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790, 1800); passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, military, passenger lists, naturalizations | Free finding aids; mixed digital/physical |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1) matching Philadelphia and the 1780–1810 window; no nextPageToken was returned, so this is the complete set. The collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections; 3 overlap with the target period and are detailed above. One collection returned (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) was labeled a synthetic test fixture and has been excluded.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Epidemic Committee records, Bush Hill hospital records, tax assessments, deed records, city administrative records | In-person or contact archives |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript epidemic sources, church register transcriptions, tax records, family papers, local histories, Benjamin Rush papers | In-person; some materials digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published transcriptions | In-person, membership; https://www.genpa.org |
| Individual church archives (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, etc.) | Original burial, baptism, and marriage registers | Contact individual church or diocesan archives |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region | Federal records for the Philadelphia area, naturalizations, federal court records | In-person in Philadelphia |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Benjamin Rush papers; colonial and early national Philadelphia materials | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports — manuscript at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized or indexed
- Bush Hill hospital patient records — manuscript; requires contact with Philadelphia City Archives
- Individual church burial registers (beyond the single Quaker volume in volume_search) — many are on FamilySearch microfilm but are not indexed; the single digitized volume is browse-only Quaker meeting minutes, not a burial register
- Philadelphia County tax assessment records for 1792–1795 — held at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as indexed online
- Pre-1906 vital records generally — no civil registration existed; all are church-held and mostly on microfilm rather than indexed online

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fires or archival destruction events for Philadelphia in the 1793 period were returned by the tools. The epidemic itself did not cause archival damage. However, no civil vital registration system existed in 1793, so individual deaths survive only through church registers and the epidemic-specific published and manuscript sources described above. This is a structural gap in the record system, not a loss event.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the starting point** for the epidemic period. The FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms church registers are the primary vital source before 1906 statewide registration. Identify the family's denomination first, then target that register.
- **Read Mathew Carey's account first** if the family was in Philadelphia in summer or fall 1793. This published source lists names of the dead and is freely available in digitized form.
- **Anticipate a probate spike.** With roughly one-tenth of the city dead in a few months, the Register of Wills was flooded in late 1793–1794. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196) covers this window but must be browsed image by image — no name index exists.
- **Pre-1854 district records.** A family in Northern Liberties, Southwark, or Germantown will have records filed under those district names, not 'Philadelphia.' Research the specific district of residence.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 censuses as anchors.** The 1790 census (3 years before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (7 years after) can bracket who was present and who survived. Both are indexed and available on Ancestry.com.
- **Search adjoining counties for refugees.** Thousands fled the city during the epidemic. The FamilySearch Philadelphia County home page returned only generic content in this survey, so neighboring county names were not confirmed from the tool results. Search records in the counties immediately surrounding Philadelphia for temporarily or permanently relocated families.
- **Use the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania indexes.** The FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) specifically names the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania as having compiled indexes to many church records — consult these before browsing unindexed registers.
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap note.** All FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Probate Records, and Land and Property returned only the generic fallback page in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for place-specific guidance that this survey could not retrieve.

- **Where held:** Historical newspapers available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) — confirmed in external_links_search curated results (subscription). The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Free Library of Philadelphia also hold newspaper collections.
- **Content value:** Death notices, epidemic victim lists, notices of orphaned children, estate settlement notices, public health announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Pre-1820 passenger lists are less detailed than later records but do exist.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization records (filed in any court of record before 1906)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) — confirmed in external_links_search results; Ancestry.com also holds digitized passenger records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children. When researching a Philadelphia family with immigrant origins, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County property tax and personal property assessment records
- **Date range:** Assessment records exist from the colonial period through the early national period
- **Substitute value:** Tax records from 1792–1793 can establish a household's presence and economic status just before the epidemic; assessments from 1794–1795 may document property changes from deaths
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds some transcriptions

### Other record types
- **Guardianship records:** With many parents dying in the epidemic, guardianship filings in the Philadelphia Orphans' Court spiked in late 1793–1794. Guardianship files are included in Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196), browse-only.
- **Almshouse and poor relief records:** The Committee appointed by citizens maintained relief records naming recipients; the Philadelphia Almshouse also kept records. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Quaker meeting records:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, browse-only). Quakers were prominent in epidemic relief efforts and documented deaths within their community.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century histories of Philadelphia often reprint early records, list founding families, and narrate the 1793 epidemic by name.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196; 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (id: 1571957; 312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (id: 1502909; 198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322; 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790, 1800); passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, military, passenger lists, naturalizations | Free finding aids; mixed digital/physical |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1) matching Philadelphia and the 1780–1810 window; no nextPageToken was returned, so this is the complete set. The collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections; 3 overlap with the target period and are detailed above. One collection returned (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) was labeled a synthetic test fixture and has been excluded.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Epidemic Committee records, Bush Hill hospital records, tax assessments, deed records, city administrative records | In-person or contact archives |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript epidemic sources, church register transcriptions, tax records, family papers, local histories, Benjamin Rush papers | In-person; some materials digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published transcriptions | In-person, membership; https://www.genpa.org |
| Individual church archives (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, etc.) | Original burial, baptism, and marriage registers | Contact individual church or diocesan archives |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region | Federal records for the Philadelphia area, naturalizations, federal court records | In-person in Philadelphia |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Benjamin Rush papers; colonial and early national Philadelphia materials | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports — manuscript at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as digitized or indexed
- Bush Hill hospital patient records — manuscript; requires contact with Philadelphia City Archives
- Individual church burial registers (beyond the single Quaker volume in volume_search) — many are on FamilySearch microfilm but are not indexed; the single digitized volume is browse-only Quaker meeting minutes, not a burial register
- Philadelphia County tax assessment records for 1792–1795 — held at Philadelphia City Archives; not confirmed as indexed online
- Pre-1906 vital records generally — no civil registration existed; all are church-held and mostly on microfilm rather than indexed online

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fires or archival destruction events for Philadelphia in the 1793 period were returned by the tools. The epidemic itself did not cause archival damage. However, no civil vital registration system existed in 1793, so individual deaths survive only through church registers and the epidemic-specific published and manuscript sources described above. This is a structural gap in the record system, not a loss event.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the starting point** for the epidemic period. The FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms church registers are the primary vital source before 1906 statewide registration. Identify the family's denomination first, then target that register.
- **Read Mathew Carey's account first** if the family was in Philadelphia in summer or fall 1793. This published source lists names of the dead and is freely available in digitized form.
- **Anticipate a probate spike.** With roughly one-tenth of the city dead in a few months, the Register of Wills was flooded in late 1793–1794. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196) covers this window but must be browsed image by image — no name index exists.
- **Pre-1854 district records.** A family in Northern Liberties, Southwark, or Germantown will have records filed under those district names, not 'Philadelphia.' Research the specific district of residence.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 censuses as anchors.** The 1790 census (3 years before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (7 years after) can bracket who was present and who survived. Both are indexed and available on Ancestry.com.
- **Search adjoining counties for refugees.** Thousands fled the city during the epidemic. The FamilySearch Philadelphia County home page returned only generic content in this survey, so neighboring county names were not confirmed from the tool results. Search records in the counties immediately surrounding Philadelphia for temporarily or permanently relocated families.
- **Use the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania indexes.** The FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) specifically names the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania as having compiled indexes to many church records — consult these before browsing unindexed registers.
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap note.** All FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Probate Records, and Land and Property returned only the generic fallback page in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for place-specific guidance that this survey could not retrieve.

---

**Chicago / Cook County — Records for Families Affected by the Great Fire of 1871**

Chicago's Cook County records for the 1860s and 1870s are shaped above all else by the Great Fire of October 1871, which burned the Cook County Courthouse and destroyed most early official records — deeds, birth and death registers, court files, probate papers, and tax rolls.

**What survived — and where:**

- **1870 U.S. Federal Census** — Intact because originals were kept in Washington, not the courthouse. This is the single most useful tool for locating families in Chicago around the fire year. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

- **FamilySearch vital records (post-fire):** Four collections cover Cook County beginning in or shortly after 1871:
  - Birth certificates (from 1871)
  - Death records (from 1871)
  - Marriage records (from 1871)
  - Church records (reaching back to 1833; 285,000+ indexed entries)

**Key substitutes for destroyed records:**

- **Burnt Record Act / Reconstructed Property Deeds** — Cook County Recorder of Deeds. After the fire, the Illinois legislature enabled property owners to reconstruct title through sworn testimony. These reconstruction deeds can sometimes replace lost deeds for establishing residency and identity.

- **Chicago Tribune missing persons & relief notices** — Post-fire issues (October–November 1871) carried extensive notices of survivors seeking family members and relief organizations listing recipients. Held at the **Newberry Library** and the **Chicago History Museum**.

- **City directories** — The Newberry Library holds an extensive run of Chicago city directories, which can bracket a family's presence in the city before and after the fire.

- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** — Held at the **Chicago History Museum**; sometimes document property ownership and occupancy.

**Repositories:**

| Repository | What they hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (online) | 1870 census, post-1871 vitals, church records | Free online |
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories, newspapers, genealogical collections | In-person / correspondence |
| Chicago History Museum | Tribune archives, insurance records, fire relief records | In-person / correspondence |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds | In-person |

**Recommended next step:** Start with the 1870 census to establish your family in Chicago before the fire, then use the post-fire vital records and church records to follow them forward. For property and court matters, the Burnt Record Act deeds and the Chicago History Museum's collections are the best substitutes for what was lost.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County was formed in 1831 (place_search dateRange: "+1831/")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this place/period. Chicago grew dramatically in this era — from a major Great Lakes commercial hub to one of the largest U.S. cities by 1880 — but specific figures cannot be cited without tool confirmation.
- **Economy:** Railroads, meatpacking, grain trade, iron/steel manufacturing, Great Lakes shipping, commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Large communities of Irish, German, Swedish, Norwegian, Polish, and Bohemian immigrants were well-established by 1870; smaller communities of English, Scottish, and Welsh settlers; a small but growing African American population
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (largest single denomination, serving Irish, German, Polish, and Bohemian immigrants), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian congregations), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most early official records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

## Boundary changes
Cook County was formed in 1831 and remained stable through the target period. No significant boundary changes affected the county between 1860 and 1885.

## The Great Fire — Record Destruction and Substitutes

This is the central fact of Cook County genealogy for this period. The fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which held deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Many church parish registers were also destroyed. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

Key substitute sources confirmed by tool results:
- **Federal census (1870):** The 1870 schedules for Chicago survived because originals were held in Washington DC, not the courthouse. This is the single most important pre-fire locating tool.
- **Burnt Record Act (1872):** Required property owners to re-register deeds; reconstructed deed records created under this law are the primary substitute for destroyed land records.
- **Church records:** Parishes outside the fire zone maintained their registers. The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic registers.
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library.
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership.
- **Chicago Tribune fire notices:** The Tribune published missing persons notices, relief lists, and fire-loss notices in the weeks after October 1871 — a unique source for displaced families.
- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records:** The Society distributed relief to fire survivors and kept records of recipients by name and former address; held at the Chicago History Museum.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch collections for Cook County birth certificates, death records, and marriage records all begin in 1871. The FamilySearch Illinois Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey and did not provide a confirmed county-level registration start date. The 1871 start of these collections likely reflects both when county-level civil registration became operational and the destruction of any earlier records in the fire. The Illinois statewide registration system was not established until the early twentieth century; the Illinois Vital Records wiki page should be consulted directly for exact dates at each level.
- **What exists (on FamilySearch, indexed + images):**
  - Birth Certificates 1871–1940: 1,450,000 records (collection ID 2024189)
  - Death Records 1871–1947: 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - Marriage Records 1871–1920: 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized, free)
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil registration records were destroyed in the fire. No confirmed earlier county-level civil series survives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1833 onward — see Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Norwegian Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Jewish congregations, Polish Catholic, Bohemian Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978), indexed + images
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic registers); FamilySearch microfilm (many series); denominational archives for Protestant congregations (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Language:** Many immigrant-congregation registers are in German, Swedish, Norwegian, Polish, or Latin (Catholic sacramental registers). Researchers must be able to read the original language.
- **Fire impact:** Many parish registers in the burn zone were destroyed. Parishes outside the zone kept intact records. The FamilySearch church records collection covers 1833–1925, so some pre-fire material was preserved or reconstructed.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for Cook County/Chicago in 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880. The 1870 schedules for Chicago survived the fire because originals were in Washington DC (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1880 census is fully indexed (Soundex and name indexes on FamilySearch and Ancestry).
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record persons who died in the year preceding each census — the 1880 mortality schedule covers deaths in 1879, not fire victims directly, but the 1870 schedule covers deaths in 1869.
- **State census:** Illinois did not conduct a state census; no intercensal enumerations are available.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, naturalizations (pre-1906 filed in any court of record), civil suits, equity proceedings
- **Fire impact:** Most pre-fire probate and court records were destroyed when the Cook County Courthouse burned (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).
- **Digitized volumes on FamilySearch:**
  - Volume 009982110: 38 images of pre-fire Cook County Court records (reconstructed copies, 1865–1871) — **browse-only images** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image)
  - Volume 009982111: 112 images of post-fire property re-recordings (1871–1880) — **partially indexed** (41% name-searchable)
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County government and court records post-1871 (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state — Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office issued original federal patents; BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds these patents online.
- **Types:** Federal patents (BLM GLO), county deeds (Cook County Recorder), reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act (1872), mortgages, tax records
- **Fire impact:** The county's deed records burned in 1871. The Burnt Record Act (1872) required re-registration; reconstructed deed books are at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds. The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a critical substitute for pre-fire ownership documentation (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (originals and reconstructed deeds); BLM GLO online for federal patents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War (1861–1865) — a large portion of Chicago-area men of military age served. The fire's 1871 date falls shortly after the war, making veterans' records a key source for identifying families and household members.
- **Record types:** Civil War Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs), pension files, Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) post records, Illinois state muster rolls, Civil War draft registrations

# Locality Guide: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County was formed in 1831 (place_search dateRange: "+1831/")
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this place/period. Chicago grew dramatically in this era — from a major Great Lakes commercial hub to one of the largest U.S. cities by 1880 — but specific figures cannot be cited without tool confirmation.
- **Economy:** Railroads, meatpacking, grain trade, iron/steel manufacturing, Great Lakes shipping, commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Large communities of Irish, German, Swedish, Norwegian, Polish, and Bohemian immigrants were well-established by 1870; smaller communities of English, Scottish, and Welsh settlers; a small but growing African American population
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (largest single denomination, serving Irish, German, Polish, and Bohemian immigrants), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian congregations), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most early official records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

## Boundary changes
Cook County was formed in 1831 and remained stable through the target period. No significant boundary changes affected the county between 1860 and 1885.

## The Great Fire — Record Destruction and Substitutes

This is the central fact of Cook County genealogy for this period. The fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which held deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Many church parish registers were also destroyed. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

- **Federal census (1870):** The 1870 schedules for Chicago survived because originals were held in Washington DC, not the courthouse. This is the single most important pre-fire locating tool.
- **Burnt Record Act (1872):** Required property owners to re-register deeds; reconstructed deed records created under this law are the primary substitute for destroyed land records.
- **Church records:** Parishes outside the fire zone maintained their registers. The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic registers.
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library.
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership.
- **Chicago Tribune fire notices:** The Tribune published missing persons notices, relief lists, and fire-loss notices in the weeks after October 1871 — a unique source for displaced families.
- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records:** The Society distributed relief to fire survivors and kept records of recipients by name and former address; held at the Chicago History Museum.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch collections for Cook County birth certificates, death records, and marriage records all begin in 1871. The FamilySearch Illinois Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey and did not provide a confirmed county-level registration start date. The 1871 start of these collections likely reflects both when county-level civil registration became operational and the destruction of any earlier records in the fire. The Illinois statewide registration system was not established until the early twentieth century; the Illinois Vital Records wiki page should be consulted directly for exact dates at each level.
- **What exists (on FamilySearch, indexed + images):**

  - Death Records 1871–1947: 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - Marriage Records 1871–1920: 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized, free)
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil registration records were destroyed in the fire. No confirmed earlier county-level civil series survives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1833 onward — see Church Records below.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Norwegian Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Jewish congregations, Polish Catholic, Bohemian Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978), indexed + images

- **Language:** Many immigrant-congregation registers are in German, Swedish, Norwegian, Polish, or Latin (Catholic sacramental registers). Researchers must be able to read the original language.

Here is the locality guide the research agent produced:

---

**Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s)**

Louisiana during the French colonial period (roughly 1699 to 1800, with Spain taking actual administrative control in 1769) left a distinctive set of records quite unlike anything in the later American archive.

**Key Record Types & Repositories**

- **Sacramental Registers (Catholic Church):** The Church was the only legally recognized institution recording births, marriages, and deaths — no civil registration existed. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans kept sacramental registers from 1720 onward.

- **French Superior Council Records:** These produced the legal backbone of the colony — land grants, estate inventories, contracts, and court proceedings that name ordinary colonists. Held today at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans.

- **Notarial Acts (1730s onward):** The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds these. Marriage contracts routinely name the parties' parents and their places of origin in France, Canada, or Germany — an invaluable source for tracing origins.

- **FamilySearch Digitized Volumes:** Two digitized collections exist covering sacramental registers and notarial acts, but both must be browsed image by image in French or Spanish — nothing is name-indexed.

- **Spanish Period Records (1769–1800):** The same families continue, but administrative language shifts. These are partially held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain.

- **French Colonial Archives:** Emigrant lists and census rolls are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** in Aix-en-Provence, France.

**Important Caveats**

- No online name search will get you very far — these records must be read in the original French or Spanish.
- A family's trail crosses both the French and Spanish administrative series without a clean break, so researchers must work both.

**Recommended Next Step**

Identify which specific family or parish to begin with, then locate the relevant sacramental register volume and work through it alongside any notarial acts or Superior Council estate records that overlap the same household.

Both FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image in French or Spanish.

The Superior Council records (land grants, estate inventories, court proceedings, contracts, 1699–1769) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans, not in major online genealogy databases.

French colonial census rolls are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France; Spanish colonial administrative records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain.

New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial acts from the 1730s (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) — marriage contracts often name parties' parents and French or Canadian places of origin.

Families near colonial Louisiana's eastern margins may have generated records in British West Florida (post-1762) — search the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the British National Archives (Kew) across that border.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was established as a French colony in 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville. France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain in the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, though Spain did not take actual administrative control until 1769. The territory was secretly retroceded to France in 1800, then sold to the United States in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (France, 1699–1762/1769), then Viceroyalty of New Spain (Spain, 1769–1800)
- **Population during period:** Population figures for Louisiana 1700–1800 were not returned by the tools.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers; Canadians; German immigrants (Côte des Allemands); Acadians arriving ca. 1755–1785 after the Grand Dérangement; African enslaved people; Native American peoples; Spanish settlers and administrators after 1769
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the Code Noir made it the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana
- **Key historical events:** 1699 — French colony established; 1718 — New Orleans founded; 1755–1785 — Acadian expulsion and Cajun settlement; 1762 — Treaty of Fontainebleau cedes colony to Spain; 1769 — Spanish administrative control begins; 1800 — retroceded to France; 1803 — Louisiana Purchase

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French colonial Louisiana administered from New Orleans, spanning the Mississippi River drainage basin.
- **1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau):** France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. Britain received the eastern bank (West Florida — present-day southern Alabama and Mississippi). Family records do not split cleanly at this date: the same Catholic parishes and notarial traditions continued, but governance and administrative language shifted.
- **1769:** Spain takes actual administrative control. The Superior Council (French) is replaced by the Cabildo (Spanish). Records transition from French to Spanish governance style; French continued in everyday use.
- **Practical implication for researchers:** A family's genealogical trail crosses both French and Spanish administrative series without a clean break. Researchers must work both series together.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed during the French colonial period. The Catholic Church was the sole institution recording vital events. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content; a Louisiana-specific civil registration start date is not stated in the returned tool results.
- **What exists:** NO government registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1700–1800. Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital records source for this entire period.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives hold original registers from 1720. FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) covers this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (enforced by the Code Noir throughout the French colonial period). St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has sacramental registers from 1720. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons, required by the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) — 987,654 records, images available. Free at FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Volume 004330991 — 264 images, sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** In French and Spanish. Must be browsed image by image. Researchers must read the original languages.
- **Physical originals:** St. Louis Cathedral and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives
- **Language:** French (1720–ca. 1769), then Spanish and French mixed (1769–1800)

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France conducted several colonial census enumerations (approximately 1699, 1706, 1721, 1724, 1726, 1727, 1732, 1737, 1745, 1766). These list heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and livestock. Administrative copies are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 — after the target period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM (physical or written request). Some may be available through the Louisiana Historical Center.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, guardianships, debt proceedings, civil suits — all conducted through the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) during the French period, and the Cabildo during the Spanish period
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — 456,789 records, images available, covering from 1756 through the late French and full Spanish colonial period.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Volume 004330992 — 149 images, French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), covering Louisiana 1699–1769. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** In French and Spanish.
- **Physical holdings:** Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories) are at the Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French colonial Louisiana used the French long-lot (arpent) system — narrow strips perpendicular to waterways, not the rectangular survey used in most of the U.S.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants (concessions) were issued by the French Crown through the Superior Council. These are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial acts (contracts, sales, mortgages, marriage settlements, property transactions)
- **Notarial Archives:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Public access available. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **American State Papers:** French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series (available online at NARA and memory.loc.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (1754–1763, ending French rule); colonial conflicts with Spain, Britain, and Native nations
- **Record types:** French colonial military rolls and muster lists; Spanish garrison records
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial military records. Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial Louisiana military records (1769–1800). Some material also at the Louisiana Historical Center.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans was established in 1789 (during the Spanish period). Earlier colonial burials were at church grounds or unmarked sites.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some New Orleans historic cemeteries; colonial-era burial coverage is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Catholic burial registers (in the sacramental register series above) are the primary source for burials in the colonial period.

### Newspaper records
- **Context:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, began publication in 1794 (Spanish period). No newspapers existed during the early French colonial period (pre-1762).
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Louisiana State Library hold some early Louisiana papers; coverage for 1700–1800 is sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant origins:** Immigrants arrived from France, Canada (especially Acadia), Germany (Côte des Allemands), and Africa (enslaved). Acadian refugees arrived ca. 1755–1785 following the Grand Dérangement.
- **Record types:** French colonial emigrant lists, concession records naming settlers' places of origin; administrative passenger lists in the ANOM.
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence holds emigration and settler records for the French colonial period.
- **Content note:** Colonial Louisiana passenger lists are administrative documents and concession records, not organized like 19th-century U.S. arrival manifests. Full family groups including children may be named.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records are embedded in Superior Council administrative proceedings and Spanish Cabildo records.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council records); ANOM (French administrative records, Aix-en-Provence)
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls and estate inventories partially substitute for missing tax rolls.

### Other record types
- **Superior Council minutes and proceedings:** Critical source for 18th-century Louisiana genealogy — names ordinary colonists in land disputes, debt cases, estate proceedings, and civil matters. At the Louisiana Historical Center. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Notarial acts (1730s onward):** Marriage contracts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center routinely name the contracting parties' parents and their places of origin in France or Canada — critical genealogical data. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Enslaved persons records:** Estate inventories and sacramental registers both name enslaved individuals. The Code Noir's baptism requirement means enslaved Africans and their descendants appear in Catholic registers from the colony's earliest years. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (1612905; 987,654 records); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (2078341; 456,789 records); 2 browse-only volumes (004330991, 004330992) in French/Spanish | Free |
| NARA | American State Papers: Public Lands (land grant documentation) | Free online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records — sparse colonial coverage | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — primarily post-1800; limited colonial coverage | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection — not applicable to the French colonial period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana in 1700–1800; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records 1699–1769 (land grants, court proceedings, estate inventories, contracts); partially digitized | In-person; written inquiry |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s: contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from St. Louis Cathedral, 1720 onward | Contact the Archdiocese |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grants and concessions | In-person / records requests |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records, emigration records | In-person; partial access at archives.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial Louisiana records 1769–1800: administrative, military, ecclesiastical | In-person; some digitized via PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) |

## Records NOT online

The following record types for the French colonial period exist but are not available in major online databases:
- French colonial census rolls (at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence)
- The bulk of Superior Council proceedings — partially at Louisiana Historical Center, not in Ancestry or FamilySearch at an indexed level
- Spanish Cabildo administrative records (1769–1800)
- Most notarial acts before the mid-19th century (at New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — must be visited in person)
- French colonial military muster rolls (at ANOM)
- Spanish colonial military and administrative records (at Archivo General de Indias, Seville)

## Known record losses

No specific record destruction events for colonial-era Louisiana records were named in the tool results returned for this survey. However, the extreme age of these records (300+ years), the tropical climate of New Orleans, and multiple changes of political authority (French to Spanish to French to U.S.) mean survival is uneven. Researchers should expect gaps in sacramental registers for smaller colonial-era parishes outside New Orleans.

## Research tips
- **No civil registration in the colonial period.** Catholic parish registers beginning with St. Louis Cathedral in 1720 are the sole vital records source. There is no government birth, marriage, or death index to search for this period. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Read French and Spanish.** Both FamilySearch digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700–1800 (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in French and Spanish. The notarial acts and Superior Council records are likewise in French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). A translator or paleographer experienced in colonial French and Spanish scripts is essential.
- **The Superior Council records are essential.** This body handled land grants, estate inventories, contracts, and civil proceedings for the entire French colonial period. Its records name ordinary colonists — not just elites — in disputes, debts, and estate settlements. Held at the Louisiana Historical Center. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Notarial acts from the 1730s name parents and origins.** Marriage contracts and estate documents at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center routinely name the contracting parties' parents and their places of origin in France, Canada, or Germany. These are often the only surviving link back to the Old World. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **France-to-Spain transition: work both series.** The 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau ceded Louisiana to Spain, but Spain did not take actual administrative control until 1769. ---

Louisiana during the French colonial period (roughly 1699 to 1800, with Spain taking actual administrative control in 1769) left a distinctive set of records quite unlike anything in the later American archive. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized institution recording births, marriages, and deaths — the colonial government created no civil registration — and St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans kept those sacramental registers from 1720 onward. The French Superior Council produced the legal backbone of the colony: land grants, estate inventories, contracts, and court proceedings that name ordinary colonists and are held today at the Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans. Notarial acts from the 1730s at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center are a goldmine because marriage contracts routinely name the parties' parents and their places of origin in France, Canada, or Germany. Two digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch covering this period (sacramental registers and notarial acts), but both must be browsed image by image in French or Spanish — nothing is name-indexed. Records from the Spanish period (1769–1800) follow the same families but shift administrative language, and are partially at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville; colonial census rolls and emigrant lists are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France. The most important warnings are that no online name search will get you very far here — these records must be read in the original French or Spanish — and that a family's trail crosses the French and Spanish administrative series without a clean break, so researchers must work both.

The next step is to decide which specific family or parish to begin with, then locate the relevant sacramental register volume and work through it alongside any notarial acts or Superior Council estate records that overlap the same household.
