added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was established as a French colony in 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville. France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain in the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, though Spain did not take actual administrative control until 1769. The territory was secretly retroceded to France in 1800, then sold to the United States in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (France, 1699–1762/1769), then Viceroyalty of New Spain (Spain, 1769–1800)
- **Population during period:** Population figures for Louisiana 1700–1800 were not returned by the tools.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers; Canadians; German immigrants (Côte des Allemands); Acadians arriving ca. 1755–1785 after the Grand Dérangement; African enslaved people; Native American peoples; Spanish settlers and administrators after 1769
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the Code Noir made it the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana
- **Key historical events:** 1699 — French colony established; 1718 — New Orleans founded; 1755–1785 — Acadian expulsion and Cajun settlement; 1762 — Treaty of Fontainebleau cedes colony to Spain; 1769 — Spanish administrative control begins; 1800 — retroceded to France; 1803 — Louisiana Purchase

## Boundary changes
- **1699–1762:** French colonial Louisiana administered from New Orleans, spanning the Mississippi River drainage basin.
- **1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau):** France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. Britain received the eastern bank (West Florida — present-day southern Alabama and Mississippi). Family records do not split cleanly at this date: the same Catholic parishes and notarial traditions continued, but governance and administrative language shifted.
- **1769:** Spain takes actual administrative control. The Superior Council (French) is replaced by the Cabildo (Spanish). Records transition from French to Spanish governance style; French continued in everyday use.
- **Practical implication for researchers:** A family's genealogical trail crosses both French and Spanish administrative series without a clean break. Researchers must work both series together.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed during the French colonial period. The Catholic Church was the sole institution recording vital events. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content; a Louisiana-specific civil registration start date is not stated in the returned tool results.
- **What exists:** NO government registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1700–1800. Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital records source for this entire period.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives hold original registers from 1720. FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) covers this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (enforced by the Code Noir throughout the French colonial period). St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has sacramental registers from 1720. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons, required by the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) — 987,654 records, images available. Free at FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Volume 004330991 — 264 images, sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** In French and Spanish. Must be browsed image by image. Researchers must read the original languages.
- **Physical originals:** St. Louis Cathedral and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives
- **Language:** French (1720–ca. 1769), then Spanish and French mixed (1769–1800)

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France conducted several colonial census enumerations (approximately 1699, 1706, 1721, 1724, 1726, 1727, 1732, 1737, 1745, 1766). These list heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and livestock. Administrative copies are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 — after the target period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM (physical or written request). Some may be available through the Louisiana Historical Center.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, guardianships, debt proceedings, civil suits — all conducted through the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) during the French period, and the Cabildo during the Spanish period
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — 456,789 records, images available, covering from 1756 through the late French and full Spanish colonial period.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Volume 004330992 — 149 images, French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), covering Louisiana 1699–1769. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** In French and Spanish.
- **Physical holdings:** Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories) are at the Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French colonial Louisiana used the French long-lot (arpent) system — narrow strips perpendicular to waterways, not the rectangular survey used in most of the U.S.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants (concessions) were issued by the French Crown through the Superior Council. These are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial acts (contracts, sales, mortgages, marriage settlements, property transactions)
- **Notarial Archives:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Public access available. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **American State Papers:** French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series (available online at NARA and memory.loc.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (1754–1763, ending French rule); colonial conflicts with Spain, Britain, and Native nations
- **Record types:** French colonial military rolls and muster lists; Spanish garrison records
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — French colonial military records. Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial Louisiana military records (1769–1800). Some material also at the Louisiana Historical Center.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans was established in 1789 (during the Spanish period). Earlier colonial burials were at church grounds or unmarked sites.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some New Orleans historic cemeteries; colonial-era burial coverage is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Catholic burial registers (in the sacramental register series above) are the primary source for burials in the colonial period.

### Newspaper records
- **Context:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, began publication in 1794 (Spanish period). No newspapers existed during the early French colonial period (pre-1762).
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Louisiana State Library hold some early Louisiana papers; coverage for 1700–1800 is sparse.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant origins:** Immigrants arrived from France, Canada (especially Acadia), Germany (Côte des Allemands), and Africa (enslaved). Acadian refugees arrived ca. 1755–1785 following the Grand Dérangement.
- **Record types:** French colonial emigrant lists, concession records naming settlers' places of origin; administrative passenger lists in the ANOM.
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence holds emigration and settler records for the French colonial period.
- **Content note:** Colonial Louisiana passenger lists are administrative documents and concession records, not organized like 19th-century U.S. arrival manifests. Full family groups including children may be named.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax and tribute records are embedded in Superior Council administrative proceedings and Spanish Cabildo records.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council records); ANOM (French administrative records, Aix-en-Provence)
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls and estate inventories partially substitute for missing tax rolls.

### Other record types
- **Superior Council minutes and proceedings:** Critical source for 18th-century Louisiana genealogy — names ordinary colonists in land disputes, debt cases, estate proceedings, and civil matters. At the Louisiana Historical Center. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Notarial acts (1730s onward):** Marriage contracts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center routinely name the contracting parties' parents and their places of origin in France or Canada — critical genealogical data. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Enslaved persons records:** Estate inventories and sacramental registers both name enslaved individuals. The Code Noir's baptism requirement means enslaved Africans and their descendants appear in Catholic registers from the colony's earliest years. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (1612905; 987,654 records); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (2078341; 456,789 records); 2 browse-only volumes (004330991, 004330992) in French/Spanish | Free |
| NARA | American State Papers: Public Lands (land grant documentation) | Free online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records — sparse colonial coverage | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — primarily post-1800; limited colonial coverage | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection — not applicable to the French colonial period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana in 1700–1800; both are detailed above. This is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records 1699–1769 (land grants, court proceedings, estate inventories, contracts); partially digitized | In-person; written inquiry |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s: contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions | In-person; public access |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from St. Louis Cathedral, 1720 onward | Contact the Archdiocese |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grants and concessions | In-person / records requests |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records, emigration records | In-person; partial access at archives.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial Louisiana records 1769–1800: administrative, military, ecclesiastical | In-person; some digitized via PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) |

## Records NOT online

The following record types for the French colonial period exist but are not available in major online databases:
- French colonial census rolls (at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence)
- The bulk of Superior Council proceedings — partially at Louisiana Historical Center, not in Ancestry or FamilySearch at an indexed level
- Spanish Cabildo administrative records (1769–1800)
- Most notarial acts before the mid-19th century (at New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — must be visited in person)
- French colonial military muster rolls (at ANOM)
- Spanish colonial military and administrative records (at Archivo General de Indias, Seville)

## Known record losses

No specific record destruction events for colonial-era Louisiana records were named in the tool results returned for this survey. However, the extreme age of these records (300+ years), the tropical climate of New Orleans, and multiple changes of political authority (French to Spanish to French to U.S.) mean survival is uneven. Researchers should expect gaps in sacramental registers for smaller colonial-era parishes outside New Orleans.

## Research tips
- **No civil registration in the colonial period.** Catholic parish registers beginning with St. Louis Cathedral in 1720 are the sole vital records source. There is no government birth, marriage, or death index to search for this period. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Read French and Spanish.** Both FamilySearch digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700–1800 (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in French and Spanish. The notarial acts and Superior Council records are likewise in French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). A translator or paleographer experienced in colonial French and Spanish scripts is essential.
- **The Superior Council records are essential.** This body handled land grants, estate inventories, contracts, and civil proceedings for the entire French colonial period. Its records name ordinary colonists — not just elites — in disputes, debts, and estate settlements. Held at the Louisiana Historical Center. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)
- **Notarial acts from the 1730s name parents and origins.** Marriage contracts and estate documents at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center routinely name the contracting parties' parents and their places of origin in France, Canada, or Germany. These are often the only surviving link back to the Old World. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **France-to-Spain transition: work both series.** The 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau ceded Louisiana to Spain, but Spain did not take actual administrative control until 1769. Records from 1762–1769 remain French-style. After 1769, governance shifted to the Cabildo. A family's trail crosses both series without a clean break — do not stop at 1762. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Colonial census rolls are in France.** French colonial census enumerations are at the ANOM, Aix-en-Provence. These place ancestors in a household for a given year and are not duplicated in U.S.-based repositories.
- **Spanish colonial records are in Spain.** Records from the Spanish period (1769–1800) are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Some are accessible via Spain's PARES digital portal.
- **Code Noir and enslaved persons.** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. Sacramental registers therefore include records of enslaved individuals by name — often the only documents naming them. Estate inventories in the Superior Council records also enumerate enslaved persons. These are primary sources for African American colonial Louisiana family research. (Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Long-lot survey system.** French colonial land was surveyed in arpent-width strips perpendicular to waterways. Colonial land descriptions reference waterfront arpents, not section-township-range — essential context for reading concession records. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)
- **Search neighboring jurisdictions.** Families near colonial Louisiana's eastern margin may have generated records in British West Florida (post-1762). The Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the British National Archives (Kew) hold West Florida colonial records; search across that border for families living in or moving through that corridor.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this county; no population figures are confirmed from tool results.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry. According to the Wikipedia Coal Region article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region), coal mining in the region expanded dramatically in the 1820s–1870s. Mining companies maintained employment records, pay ledgers, and accident reports.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant populations drawn by the mines, including Irish, Welsh, German, and later Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants (Wikipedia, Coal Region: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (serving Irish and Eastern European immigrant miners), Welsh Baptist, Welsh Congregational, Methodist (Welsh and English miners), German Lutheran and Reformed, and later Polish Catholic, Slovak Catholic, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, and Eastern Orthodox congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Anthracite coal boom 1820s–1870s; Molly Maguires labor violence 1860s–1870s; formation of the United Mine Workers of America 1890.

## Boundary changes

- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout the target period (formed 1811).
- The neighboring coal county of Lackawanna was formed from Luzerne County in 1878; FamilySearch volume results show Lackawanna-specific mining records beginning that year (volume 002240017). Records for the Scranton area before 1878 are held under Luzerne County.
- The broader anthracite coal region spans Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Wikipedia, Coal Region).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906** (statewide level). Before that date, vital events were recorded by churches, some individual counties (Philadelphia from 1860, Allegheny from 1870 — not Schuylkill specifically), and in family Bibles. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records
- **Marriage records:** Kept at the **county level** from the colonial period — marriage licenses and bonds are at the county courthouse. FamilySearch has microfilmed many county marriage records. Source: same page.
- **What is indexed on FamilySearch:**
  - Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317): 524,189 records — **indexed + images** — overlaps the target period for 1885–1900
  - Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957): 312,045 records — **indexed + images**
  - Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909): 198,765 records — **index only** (no images)
  - Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317): 4.2 million records — **indexed + images** — post-period for late 1800s events, but useful for anyone who survived into the 1900s
- **Gaps:** Birth records before 1906 are not available through civil registration for Schuylkill County. Rely on church baptismal registers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Irish, Eastern European), Welsh Baptist, Welsh Congregational, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Polish Catholic, Slovak Catholic, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Eastern Orthodox
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Diocese of Allentown (successor to Diocese of Philadelphia) for Catholic records; denominational archives for Protestant records; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers
- **Note:** One result in collections_search (ID SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records") was explicitly labeled "synthetic test fixture" in the tool output. It is excluded from this guide's findings. Do not rely on it until independently verified at FamilySearch.org.
- **Language:** English for most Protestant records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials).

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 are all available and indexed for Schuylkill County on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921 — see Known Record Losses below.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses included mortality schedules listing deaths in the year preceding each enumeration. These are particularly valuable for this county given the absence of pre-1906 death registration.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census for this period was confirmed by tool results.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed on both FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; also naturalizations, civil suits, and county court minutes
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811) onward
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills (Pottsville) holds originals. FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3.2 million images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image; knowing the approximate date range helps limit browsing.
- **Naturalization:** Before September 1906, naturalizations were filed in any court of record — county courts of common pleas, state courts, or federal district courts. Check the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas records at the courthouse.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's original grants (1681) onward. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax assessment lists (tax duplicates survive from as early as the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties)
- **Date range:** County deed books begin at Schuylkill County formation in 1811; earlier land patents are at the Pennsylvania Land Office.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) for deed books; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for Land Office records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898); pension files from both conflicts are genealogically valuable throughout the 1870s–1900s
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (which name wives, children, and dates), draft registrations, bounty land warrants (Civil War era)
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records, original); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic and Protestant cemeteries throughout Schuylkill County; ethnic fraternal organization cemeteries for immigrant communities
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Schuylkill County cemeteries with headstone photographs — free access
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual cemeteries; some held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Pottsville Republican and other Schuylkill County newspapers published obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) for digitized historical newspapers; Pennsylvania State Library may hold microfilm of local papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate settlements, sheriff's sales), mining accident reports

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania-bound immigrants; New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island 1892–1957) was also heavily used by the coal region's immigrant communities
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch; naturalization records at county courts (pre-1906)
- **Where held:** NARA holds originals; FamilySearch and Ancestry.com have indexed arrivals
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Important:** The coal region's Irish, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, and Italian immigrants frequently appear under anglicized or phonetically respelled surnames in American records. Search under multiple spelling variants.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County tax assessment lists (tax duplicates) and property tax records
- **Date range:** Schuylkill County records from 1811; some Pennsylvania counties have tax lists surviving from the colonial period
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives; some series transcribed by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County
- **Substitute value:** Useful as census substitutes, especially for the 1890s decade where the federal census is destroyed

### Occupational / mining records

These are a critical source type for Pennsylvania coal mining families and are not typically found in standard genealogical surveys:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards — Schuylkill County, 1870–1900 (FamilySearch volume 002240015):** 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** (indexed + images). This is the most accessible digitized mining record for this county and period. Start here for any adult male mine worker.
- **Mine Accident Reports — Luzerne County, 1870–1895 (FamilySearch volume 002240016):** 287 images, **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers — Lackawanna County, 1878–1900 (FamilySearch volume 002240017):** 199 images, **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image. Note: Lackawanna County records begin in 1878 because the county was formed from Luzerne that year.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg):** Holds Mine Inspector reports from 1870 (per Wikipedia Coal Region article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region).
- **Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton:** Preserves mining community records for the broader coal region.
- **Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville:** Preserves local records including company records, community histories, and genealogical files.

**Volume survey coverage:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes matching this place and period. Only the 3 volumes detailed above represent the first page of results. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey. The researcher should retrieve additional pages from the FamilySearch catalog for a complete picture.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records, index only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); Mine Worker Employment Cards Schuylkill 1870–1900 (410 images, 95% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all available census years for Schuylkill County) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and headstone photographs | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper digitization including local Schuylkill County papers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Original passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalization records, military service and pension records | Free (in-person); some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes match this place and period in the FamilySearch volume catalog; the 3 volumes detailed above are only the first page. The full scope of digitized FamilySearch holdings for this county and period has not been examined in this survey.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, Register of Wills (probate), marriage licenses, court minutes, naturalizations | In-person or written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, Mine Inspector reports (from 1870), state-level records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, tax lists, newspaper collections, community genealogical files | In-person; contact for hours |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records for the broader coal region | In-person; contact for access |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County parishes | Written request |

## Records NOT online

- Schuylkill County birth records before 1906 (no statewide civil registration; these events are in church baptismal registers, which may or may not be microfilmed or digitized)
- Schuylkill County death records before 1906 (same situation — rely on church burial registers and census mortality schedules)
- Most naturalization records filed at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas before 1906
- Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne, 1870–1895) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna, 1878–1900) — both are digitized images on FamilySearch but have no name index and are not full-text searchable
- The 20 additional digitized volumes not yet examined from the FamilySearch volume catalog

## Known record losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. For Schuylkill County in the 1890s, substitute sources are the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses, the 1880 mortality schedules, county tax assessment lists, local borough/city directories, and church records from that decade.
- No courthouse fire or other major record loss specific to Schuylkill County was identified in the tool results for this survey. Always confirm with the Historical Society of Schuylkill County whether a specific record series is intact before concluding records do not exist.

## Research tips

- **Vital registration level and date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1906 at the statewide level. For late 1800s events in Schuylkill County, the primary sources are church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers and county marriage records. Do not expect to find a civil birth or death certificate for someone born or dying in Schuylkill County before 1906. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records
- **Land office, not BLM/GLO:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state. Land patents, warrants, and surveys are at the Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg), not the federal Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records used for federal public-land states. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records
- **Start with Mine Worker Employment Cards:** For any adult male mine worker in Schuylkill County 1870–1900, FamilySearch volume 002240015 (95% name-indexed, full-text searchable) is the most accessible digitized occupational record and should be an early step.
- **Probate requires browsing:** Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) must be browsed image by image — identify the county and approximate decade before searching to keep the task manageable.
- **Immigrant surnames:** Coal region families from Ireland, Poland, Slovakia, Lithuania, Ukraine, and Italy appear under anglicized or respelled versions of their original surnames. Generate and search multiple variant spellings.
- **Cross-county research:** Families living near the boundaries of Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland, or Luzerne counties may have generated records in adjacent jurisdictions. The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool did not return place-specific neighboring county information in this survey; verify boundaries with a historical map. The Anthracite Heritage Museum in Scranton also covers the broader multi-county coal region.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization is scattered:** Before September 1906, naturalization could be filed in any court of record — county, state, or federal. Check the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia), and any other courts where the immigrant had contact.
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap:** All four wiki_place_page sections for both Schuylkill County and Pennsylvania returned only generic fallback content in this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for the actual place-specific research pages, which likely contain additional detail not captured here.

- **Gaps:** Birth records before 1906 are not available through civil registration for Schuylkill County. Rely on church baptismal registers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Irish, Eastern European), Welsh Baptist, Welsh Congregational, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Polish Catholic, Slovak Catholic, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Eastern Orthodox
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Diocese of Allentown (successor to Diocese of Philadelphia) for Catholic records; denominational archives for Protestant records; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers
- **Note:** One result in collections_search (ID SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records") was explicitly labeled "synthetic test fixture" in the tool output. It is excluded from this guide's findings. Do not rely on it until independently verified at FamilySearch.org.
- **Language:** English for most Protestant records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials).

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 are all available and indexed for Schuylkill County on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921 — see Known Record Losses below.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses included mortality schedules listing deaths in the year preceding each enumeration. These are particularly valuable for this county given the absence of pre-1906 death registration.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census for this period was confirmed by tool results.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed on both FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; also naturalizations, civil suits, and county court minutes
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811) onward
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills (Pottsville) holds originals. FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3.2 million images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image; knowing the approximate date range helps limit browsing.
- **Naturalization:** Before September 1906, naturalizations were filed in any court of record — county courts of common pleas, state courts, or federal district courts. Check the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas records at the courthouse.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's original grants (1681) onward. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax assessment lists (tax duplicates survive from as early as the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties)
- **Date range:** County deed books begin at Schuylkill County formation in 1811; earlier land patents are at the Pennsylvania Land Office.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) for deed books; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for Land Office records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898); pension files from both conflicts are genealogically valuable throughout the 1870s–1900s
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (which name wives, children, and dates), draft registrations, bounty land warrants (Civil War era)
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records, original); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic and Protestant cemeteries throughout Schuylkill County; ethnic fraternal organization cemeteries for immigrant communities
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Schuylkill County cemeteries with headstone photographs — free access
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual cemeteries; some held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Pottsville Republican and other Schuylkill County newspapers published obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) for digitized historical newspapers; Pennsylvania State Library may hold microfilm of local papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate settlements, sheriff's sales), mining accident reports

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania-bound immigrants; New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island 1892–1957) was also heavily used by the coal region's immigrant communities
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch; naturalization records at county courts (pre-1906)
- **Where held:** NARA holds originals; FamilySearch and Ancestry.com have indexed arrivals
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Important:** The coal region's Irish, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, and Italian immigrants frequently appear under anglicized or phonetically respelled surnames in American records. Search under multiple spelling variants.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County tax assessment lists (tax duplicates) and property tax records
- **Date range:** Schuylkill County records from 1811; some Pennsylvania counties have tax lists surviving from the colonial period
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives; some series transcribed by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County
- **Substitute value:** Useful as census substitutes, especially for the 1890s decade where the federal census is destroyed

### Occupational / mining records

These are a critical source type for Pennsylvania coal mining families and are not typically found in standard genealogical surveys:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards — Schuylkill County, 1870–1900 (FamilySearch volume 002240015):** 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** (indexed + images). This is the most accessible digitized mining record for this county and period. Start here for any adult male mine worker.
- **Mine Accident Reports — Luzerne County, 1870–1895 (FamilySearch volume 002240016):** 287 images, **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers — Lackawanna County, 1878–1900 (FamilySearch volume 002240017):** 199 images, **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image. Note: Lackawanna County records begin in 1878 because the county was formed from Luzerne that year.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg):** Holds Mine Inspector reports from 1870 (per Wikipedia Coal Region article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region).
- **Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton:** Preserves mining community records for the broader coal region.
- **Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville:** Preserves local records including company records, community histories, and genealogical files.

**Volume survey coverage:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes matching this place and period. Only the 3 volumes detailed above represent the first page of results. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey. The researcher should retrieve additional pages from the FamilySearch catalog for a complete picture.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records, index only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); Mine Worker Employment Cards Schuylkill 1870–1900 (410 images, 95% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all available census years for Schuylkill County) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and headstone photographs | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper digitization including local Schuylkill County papers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Original passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalization records, military service and pension records | Free (in-person); some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes match this place and period in the FamilySearch volume catalog; the 3 volumes detailed above are only the first page. The full scope of digitized FamilySearch holdings for this county and period has not been examined in this survey.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, Register of Wills (probate), marriage licenses, court minutes, naturalizations | In-person or written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, Mine Inspector reports (from 1870), state-level records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, tax lists, newspaper collections, community genealogical files | In-person; contact for hours |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records for the broader coal region | In-person; contact for access |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County parishes | Written request |

## Records NOT online

- Schuylkill County birth records before 1906 (no statewide civil registration; these events are in church baptismal registers, which may or may not be microfilmed or digitized)
- Schuylkill County death records before 1906 (same situation — rely on church burial registers and census mortality schedules)
- Most naturalization records filed at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas before 1906
- Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne, 1870–1895) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna, 1878–1900) — both are digitized images on FamilySearch but have no name index and are not full-text searchable
- The 20 additional digitized volumes not yet examined from the FamilySearch volume catalog

## Known record losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. For Schuylkill County in the 1890s, substitute sources are the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses, the 1880 mortality schedules, county tax assessment lists, local borough/city directories, and church records from that decade.
- No courthouse fire or other major record loss specific to Schuylkill County was identified in the tool results for this survey. Always confirm with the Historical Society of Schuylkill County whether a specific record series is intact before concluding records do not exist.

## Research tips

- **Vital registration level and date:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1906 at the statewide level. For late 1800s events in Schuylkill County, the primary sources are church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers and county marriage records. Do not expect to find a civil birth or death certificate for someone born or dying in Schuylkill County before 1906. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records
- **Land office, not BLM/GLO:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state. Land patents, warrants, and surveys are at the Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg), not the federal Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records used for federal public-land states. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records
- **Start with Mine Worker Employment Cards:** For any adult male mine worker in Schuylkill County 1870–1900, FamilySearch volume 002240015 (95% name-indexed, full-text searchable) is the most accessible digitized occupational record and should be an early step.
- **Probate requires browsing:** Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) must be browsed image by image — identify the county and approximate decade before searching to keep the task manageable.
- **Immigrant surnames:** Coal region families from Ireland, Poland, Slovakia, Lithuania, Ukraine, and Italy appear under anglicized or respelled versions of their original surnames. Generate and search multiple variant spellings.
- **Cross-county research:** Families living near the boundaries of Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland, or Luzerne counties may have generated records in adjacent jurisdictions. The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool did not return place-specific neighboring county information in this survey; verify boundaries with a historical map. The Anthracite Heritage Museum in Scranton also covers the broader multi-county coal region.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization is scattered:** Before September 1906, naturalization could be filed in any court of record — county, state, or federal. Check the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia), and any other courts where the immigrant had contact.
- **FamilySearch Wiki gap:** All four wiki_place_page sections for both Schuylkill County and Pennsylvania returned only generic fallback content in this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for the actual place-specific research pages, which likely contain additional detail not captured here.

Here is what the locality guide returned:

---

Massachusetts in the early 1600s is unusual in how much survives: the colony required every town to record births, marriages, and deaths from **1639 onward**, making these town clerk records among the oldest civil vital records in North America, and they are largely available and searchable online through FamilySearch. Three overlapping FamilySearch collections cover the period — **town vital records, church records, and probate records** — alongside two digitized volumes of town meeting land records and Suffolk County church admissions, though both volumes must be browsed image by image with no name search.

Two critical points to keep in mind:

1. **Plymouth Colony vs. Massachusetts Bay Colony** were completely separate governments with entirely separate records throughout most of this period, so you must determine which colony applied before searching.
2. **Records were kept at the individual town level**, not the county or state — any search must be aimed at the specific town your ancestor lived in.

The **New England Historic Genealogical Society's Great Migration study series** is the essential finding aid for anyone whose ancestor arrived between 1620 and 1643 and needs to trace them back to England.

---

When you're ready to move from this record survey to a structured research plan targeting specific ancestors, the **research-plan** workflow is the logical next step.

quirks: Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) was a completely separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay Colony -- its records are published and indexed separately; search both when the ancestral place is unclear.
Vital records were mandated at the town level from 1639 -- route all vital record searches to the specific town of residence, not the county or state level.
The Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns; check this series before searching original manuscripts.
The NEHGS Great Migration study series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 -- the primary finding aid for tracing immigrants to their English origins.

Dates before 14 September 1752 may use Old Style (Julian) dating with New Year on 25 March; January-March events can appear one year earlier than expected -- note double dates such as 1699/1700 when transcribing.
Congregational church membership admissions are a separate record series from baptism registers -- search both when tracing adults who relocated between towns.
King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted many central and western Massachusetts towns; check for gaps in town vital and meeting records covering the mid-1670s.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company. Plymouth Colony, a separate earlier English settlement, was established in 1620 and maintained its own governmental and record-keeping structure until it merged with the Bay Colony in 1691 to form the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (seat of the Bay Colony government); Plymouth (seat of Plymouth Colony). Each county had its own seat.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Bay Colony during the Great Migration of 1630-1640 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony). The place_population tool returned no figures for this period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, timber, and coastal trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers, primarily from East Anglia.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church. Small numbers of Quakers, Baptists, and Anglicans were present, often under legal restrictions.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630-1640); Pequot War (1637); King Philip's War (1675-1676); Salem witchcraft persecutions (1692).

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) was a completely separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay Colony throughout the target period. It maintained its own courts, vital records, and land records. The two merged in 1691. Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- Within the Bay Colony, counties were organized progressively from the 1640s (Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, Suffolk, and others). Land, probate, and court records follow the county that existed at the date of the transaction.
- Maine (Province of Maine) was at various times attached to Massachusetts jurisdiction, creating records in Massachusetts archives for what is now a different state.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the colony starting in **1639** -- among the earliest mandatory civil registration in North America. Registration was at the **town** level, not county or state (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records; Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony).
- **What exists:** Birth, marriage, and death entries in town clerk records from 1639 onward.
- **Published abstractions:** The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is a critical finding aid (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** Original records at town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives, Boston.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550) -- indexed + images; approximately 3,456,789 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** No civil registration before 1639. Individual town records may be incomplete.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church Records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church from the colony's founding. Quaker, Baptist, and Anglican congregations also present.

Massachusetts in the early 1600s is unusual in how much survives: the colony required every town to record births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward, making these town clerk records among the oldest civil vital records in North America, and they are largely available and searchable online through FamilySearch. entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company. Plymouth Colony, a separate earlier English settlement, was established in 1620 and maintained its own governmental and record-keeping structure until it merged with the Bay Colony in 1691 to form the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (seat of the Bay Colony government); Plymouth (seat of Plymouth Colony). Each county had its own seat.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Bay Colony during the Great Migration of 1630-1640 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony). The place_population tool returned no figures for this period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, timber, and coastal trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers, primarily from East Anglia.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church. Small numbers of Quakers, Baptists, and Anglicans were present, often under legal restrictions.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630-1640); Pequot War (1637); King Philip's War (1675-1676); Salem witchcraft persecutions (1692).

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) was a completely separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay Colony throughout the target period. It maintained its own courts, vital records, and land records. The two merged in 1691. Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- Within the Bay Colony, counties were organized progressively from the 1640s (Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, Suffolk, and others). Land, probate, and court records follow the county that existed at the date of the transaction.
- Maine (Province of Maine) was at various times attached to Massachusetts jurisdiction, creating records in Massachusetts archives for what is now a different state.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the colony starting in **1639** -- among the earliest mandatory civil registration in North America. Registration was at the **town** level, not county or state (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records; Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony).
- **What exists:** Birth, marriage, and death entries in town clerk records from 1639 onward.
- **Published abstractions:** The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is a critical finding aid (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** Original records at town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives, Boston.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550) -- indexed + images; approximately 3,456,789 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** No civil registration before 1639. Individual town records may be incomplete.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church Records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church from the colony's founding. Quaker, Baptist, and Anglican congregations also present.
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary actions including excommunications and admonishments (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** Many early church records published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications. Originals may be held by surviving churches, denominational archives, or the Massachusetts Archives.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657) -- indexed + images; approximately 987,654 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612045 -- Suffolk County, 1630-1700: Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 121 images. **Full-text searchable, but NOT name-indexed** -- text can be searched but records cannot be browsed by person name alone.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Puritan Congregational practice recorded adult church membership admissions as a distinct series from baptisms. Both series should be searched.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Begins in 1790 -- entirely outside the 1620-1700 target window.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No colonial census of Massachusetts was returned by tools for this period. Town tax (rate) lists and militia musters partially substitute.
- **Tax/rate lists:** Town meetings recorded lists of freeholders and ratepayers; these survive as rate lists at the Massachusetts Archives and in published town histories.
- **Note:** The Massachusetts_Census FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; consult the wiki directly for any colonial enumeration details.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions.
- **Date range:** County probate records begin in the **1630s** (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** County probate courts; records also at the Massachusetts Archives. Published abstracts exist for many counties.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901) -- indexed + images; approximately 567,890 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Court records:** The General Court (colony legislature) and county courts of sessions and quarter sessions handled civil and criminal matters. Court minutes and files survive at the Massachusetts Archives from the 1620s (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. Land was allotted by town proprietors in the colonial period; town proprietary records document original land grants.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, proprietary allotments, town meeting votes on land, mortgage records.
- **Date range:** County-level deed recording from the **1630s**, surviving in remarkably complete runs (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds. The Massachusetts Archives holds colonial grants.
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612044 -- Massachusetts, 1620-1698: Town meeting and proprietors' records, 188 images. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) -- must be browsed image by image.
- **Note:** The Massachusetts_Land_and_Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Land_and_Property directly.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1637); King Philip's War (1675-1676).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, company lists, and published compilations of colonial military service.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds original colonial militia and war records. Published compilations exist for King Philip's War participants.
- **Note:** King Philip's War caused displacement of many families and possible local record losses; check for gaps in town records covering the mid-1670s.

### Cemetery records
- **Context:** Early Massachusetts cemeteries were typically town burying grounds or churchyard cemeteries attached to Congregational meeting houses.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides headstone transcriptions for many colonial-era Massachusetts cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial lists, where they survive, are held by town clerks or local historical societies.
- **Note:** Many 17th-century grave markers have not survived. Church burial registers may document burials for which no headstone remains.

### Newspaper records
- **Context:** Newspapers were not a practical source for this period. The first colonial newspaper appeared briefly in 1690 (Publick Occurrences) and was immediately suppressed. The Boston News-Letter began in 1704, outside the target window.
- No FamilySearch newspaper collections overlapping 1620-1700 were returned for Massachusetts.

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Primary event:** The Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers to Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1630-1640 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony).
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists from English ports (pre-departure records), colonial arrival lists, and published compilations.
- **FamilySearch collection note:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) begins in 1820 and does NOT cover the 1620-1700 window.
- **Primary finding aid:** The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643, their origins, and evidence for English birthplaces -- the most important resource for tracing immigrants (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests from this era record all persons aboard including families traveling together; examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rate lists (property and poll taxes) levied by colonial towns.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) and town archives; many published in local histories.
- **Substitute value:** Rate lists can place a person in a specific town in off-census years and confirm residence.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Votes and minutes document land allotments, appointments of town officers, and community decisions. Volume 007612044 contains 188 images of Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records (1620-1698), browse-only.
- **Colony court records:** Massachusetts Archives holds proceedings of the Court of Assistants and General Court from the 1620s (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Published local histories:** 19th-century county and town histories often reprint early records and list founding families -- frequently the only surviving transcription of lost records.
- **NEHGS manuscript collections:** The New England Historic Genealogical Society holds extensive manuscript collections and published genealogies (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (2061550); Church Records 1630-1920 (1921657); Probate Records 1635-1991 (1678901) | Free |
| AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration study series; manuscript collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records (mostly outside 1620-1700 window) | Free / in-person |
| Fold3 | Military records (mostly post-1700) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts 1620-1700; both are detailed above and no nextPageToken was returned, so this is the complete set. collections_search returned 5 collections for Massachusetts; 3 overlap the 1620-1700 window (detailed above); 2 fall entirely outside the window (Passenger Lists 1820-1891 and Naturalization Records 1790-1906). The external_links_search returned 6 results but with an empty standardPlace field, suggesting generic rather than Massachusetts-specific curated links.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, court records, rate lists, militia records from 1620s | In-person; some finding aids online |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, Great Migration study series, vital records abstractions | In-person research library; AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County Registries of Deeds | Land deeds from the 1630s in complete runs | In-person; some counties digitized early deed books |
| County Probate Courts / Massachusetts Archives | Probate records from the 1630s | In-person |
| Town Clerk Offices | Original town vital records | Contact individual town clerk |
| Local Historical Societies | Town meeting minutes, rate lists, genealogical manuscripts | Contact individual society |

## Records NOT online
- Town proprietors' records beyond the 188-image browse-only volume 007612044
- Colonial court records (Court of Assistants, county courts of sessions) -- at Massachusetts Archives; extent of digitization not confirmed by tools in this survey
- Town rate lists and militia musters -- largely at Massachusetts Archives or published in town histories
- Pre-1820 immigration and passenger records -- scattered, mostly available only in published compilations
- Church records not captured in collection 1921657

## Known record losses
- No specific Massachusetts-wide record destruction events were returned by tools for this period.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) disrupted many towns in central and western Massachusetts; some local records may have been lost or damaged.
- Plymouth Colony records are a distinct series; researchers searching only Bay Colony records will miss events in Plymouth jurisdiction.

## Research tips
- The Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony were two distinct jurisdictions throughout most of this period. Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) maintained separate courts, vital records, land records, and probate courts. Its records are published and indexed separately. Always determine which colony jurisdiction applied before routing a search (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- Vital records are held at the **town** level. Begin with the Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series for the specific town of interest (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- The NEHGS Great Migration study series is the single most important finding aid for the 1620-1643 immigrant generation. If your ancestor arrived before 1643, this is the first stop after the FamilySearch collections (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- Dates before 14 September 1752 may use Old Style (Julian) dating with New Year on 25 March. January-March events can appear one year earlier than expected in modern reckoning. Look for double dates such as "1699/1700" in colonial records.
- Congregational church membership admissions are a separate record series from baptism registers. Search both when tracing adults who moved between towns.
- All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) for Massachusetts returned only generic fallback content in this survey, as did the six constructed-URL topic pages (Vital_Records, Church_Records, Land_and_Property, Probate_Records, Census, Naming_Customs). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki for Massachusetts directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy

Here is the locality guide for Oklahoma Land Run research:

---

Oklahoma in the Land Run era divides into **two separate record-keeping worlds**: Oklahoma Territory (the settler counties organized in May 1890) and Indian Territory (the Five Civilized Tribes' lands), which coexisted until statehood in November 1907.

## Key Records & Repositories

### 1. Federal Homestead Entry Files
The most important record for any Land Run family. Held at the **National Archives** and freely searchable at the **Bureau of Land Management's GLO Records website**. Each file names the claimant, neighboring witnesses, and details of the land claim.

### 2. 1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census
The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed, but **Oklahoma Territory's own 1890 special territorial census** — one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the country — is held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** and documents the earliest settlers.

### 3. Dawes Commission Enrollment Records (1898–1914)
Essential for anyone with family connections to the **Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, or Seminole nations**. Held at the **National Archives**; FamilySearch has the images (browse only, not indexed).

---

## Critical Pitfall
Most Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, and Missouri**. Their origins won't be found in Oklahoma documents — pre-Oklahoma records in those origin states will be essential for tracing families back further.

## Suggested Next Steps
Start with the homestead file and the 1900 federal census to establish where the family settled, then work backward through the origin state's records.
